The Grand Trunk Railway Company have been very slow in extending their line. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson), have built, within the last twenty years, 1,100 miles of road, including four important bridges, at an outlay of $35,000,000, without one dollar of aid from the government of this country. Now I want to refer to their mileage. They have a very recent history, they are not an old road. Their main line was 2.905 miles long from Vancouver to Montreal ; but since their inception as a road their total mileage has increased to S.fMOJ. Well, what about the Grand Trunk ? The Grand Trunk Company have increased their mileage very slowly in this country, and I want to point out that the policy of the Grand Trunk that has prevailed in the past in this respect is very likely to continue in the future. No one who looks into that agreement but must see that the fact of their getting $25,000,000 of stock will give them a control to that extent that nobody else will have the right to interfere with. The old Grand Trunk will still be the dominant Influence in reference to the now :oad, and if they are still the dominant influence in the policy of the new road, there will be nothing like the branch lines reaching out into new sections such as the Canadian Pacific Railway system has constructed, notwithstanding the efforts of hon. gentlemen opposite to put obstacles in their way. This is a very important matter for us to consider. What is the condition of things ? Why, go back to the 80's, and see what the Grand Trunk were doing ? When there was a charter granted for a road called the Ontario and Quebec Railway, upon which there were grants by governments and municipalities of no less than $1,000,000, what did the Grand Trunk do ? They bought that charter, if I remember correctly, at a cost of some $34,000, notwithstanding that tnere were $1,000,000 attached to that charter by way of bonuses and grants which they allowed to lapse. What for ? For the pur pose of hindering the Canadian Pacific Rail way getting from Toronto to Smith's Falls. When you travel over the Canadian Pacific Railway in the neighbourhood of Perth you will notice a road graded, but which never went any further, that is the road I refer to.
Who was the man who helped to do that mischief ? Senator Cox was the man who came in to buy up that road and kill the interests of the locality between Smith's Falls and Toronto. The Canadian Pacific Railway built the road at their own expense notwithstanding the fact that the Grand Trunk tried to block the undertaking. We have a perfect right to consider these things and to consider how far the influence of Senator Cox may permeate this new proposition. We find from their report of 1884, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company owned 1,5301 miles, that they part owned and had under lease 53Sf miles and that they had under lease 843 miles of road. In 1892 they only owned 2,981 miles, and I want to draw the attention of the House and of the country to the fact that the largest outlay in improvements and extensions lias been made not in Canada but in the United States. Their enormous outlay has been made in American territory in making extensions in order to carry out their business. Does anybody pretend to say that with that great outlay the proposition that the government are now making is going to remedy all the difficulties that exist in this country in reference to railway rates and railway busi-

ness 7 The Grand Trunk Railway have gone very slowly in the matter of railway extension in this country and now the government are building a road and giving it to them. The hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell) was good enough to say, that we ought to be thankful to be able to unload this scheme on the Grand Trunk Railway which means that if this turns out to be a bad bargain it is ours because we stand behind it. If the horse is lame we must keep it; that is what it means. After we do unload it it will come back to us, if it is no good to the Grand' Trunk Pacific Railway Company. The guarantee that the government proposes to give to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company by this measure carries with it an obligation which the government cannot say does not amount to anything. Why do you give them a guarantee if this road is any good 7 Are you not giving them a guarantee in order that they may finance the undertaking and because of the possibility that they may not be able to meet their obligations 7 It is because of that contingency that the government steps in and gives them a guarantee. I want to call the attention of the House to the form of guarantee which has been given by the French government to the railways in France. They have changed their system in France because of political changes and of the financial difficulties of 1881. They have about six companies which control the l'ailways of France ail converging at Paris and each company is allowed a certain territory in the country. The policy of the government has been to guarantee the earnings of these roads and not the interest on the bonds which means virtually that the roads will always be in a position to pay their obligations as far as interest is concerned. There is only one road and that is the Northern road running through a portion of France that represents fifty-three per cent of the population that has not called upon the government to carry out the guarantee. What does any sensible man thiuk of this proposed road running through a country where there are no people 7 Does any sensible man mean to say that tills obligation assumed by the government does not mean anything 7 To show how little idea the government and their friends have as to what it means, we have only to refer to the argument used yesterday by the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) who compared the interest charged on the road to be built under this proposed scheme with the total cost of the road under the scheme proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax). He represented that the cost of one would be .$13,000,000 and that the other would be $200,000,000. If the hon. gentleman would figure out the total outlay involved in the scheme proposed by his friends he would be surprised at the result to which his arithmetic would lead him. No reason-Mr. BRODER.
able man can claim that you can go through tlie province of New Brunswick and construct a suitable road ten or fifteen miles north of the present railway where there is a difference between the valleys and the tops of the ridges of from 1,000 to 1,200 feet. If you are going to give cheaper freight rates you will have to construct a road that will cost $75,000 per mile. Then, hon. gentlemen opposite talk about the water-powers on the height of land. Even the right hon. leader of the government and the hon. Minister of Finance talked about the water-powers away up on the height of land. Who ever heard of water-powers where the rivers start upon their courses 7 What rubbish to give the country ? Water-powers away up the height of land where the rivers take their rise. Water-powers 7 You cau go out from t-lie city of Ottawa only a few miles and find enormous water-powers undeveloped. Why do not hon. gentlemen give their attention to the water-powers nearer home 7 Right on the Ottawa river thousands upon thousands of horse power are going to waste and nobody is saying anything about them. Yet, these hon. gentlemen are proposing to spend millions of money to reach the water-powers away up in the north country when nobody wants to use them. The only reasonable solution of the question to my mind is to utilize the railways that we have now in existence. We have now no less than seven different roads running from the main lines northward between Lake St. John and Lake Nipissing. These roads have received considerable government aid. Why do not hon. gentlemen opposite a'dopt the policy of extending these roads into the northern country and encouraging people from the present settlements to go up into that country 7 Bring them nearer the source of supply and let them procure their supplies and send out their products in this way instead of running a road 1,800 miles from Winnipeg to Moncton. That is a great scheme. It is a great national scheme and no great nation would ever touch It. The great national scheme ought to be the solution of the transportation question in the interests of the people of this country. Then, there was a bugaboo raised about the bonding privilege. The right hon. leader of the government based his whole argument upon the fact that the bonding privilege might be taken away. Let anybody go and look up the interstate commerce report and find what they say about that matter. Then we have in the other House a gentleman who has but lately been elevated from this House to the other by the right hon. gentleman. He is talking about war with the United States. He says that the United States want to go to war, that they are getting ready for it. It occurred to me that if the hon. gentleman is serious, and the government, of course, endorse him as one of their supporters, we ought to get a minister of war instead of a

Minister of Militia. The lion. Minister of Militia and Defence (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) is too peaceful and kindhearted a man for that. He will never be able, to till that place properly during this terrible war that is coming on us from the United States An hon. Senator talking in the other House only yesterday about the United States going to war insisted on the building of this road. The need for this road is that the United States is going to war. What are you going to do with that road in war time ? Are you going to send your troops out there to meet the United States ? The probability is that the hon. gentleman wanted to take to the woods if there should be trouble and wanted that road to get there. Most of the hon. gentlemen opposite would do so after all the loyalty we have heard about. Such nonsense to be talked by serious men ; war, taking away the bonding privileges ! Does not any reasonable man know that there is no one as much interested in the bonding privileges as the United States. New England particularly, and the railways of the United States also are more interested twice over than Canada. If we look at that aspect of the question the only true solution of our position is to run lines north and and give back to the front settlements that now exist. The only possible way-and I am speaking of peaceful avocation, I am not speaking of war-the only successful way to compete with the influence of American commerce is to give more breadth to the present country; is to give feed to the centres that now exist from the north country in the rear and you can only do that by running railways into that northern country and opening up settlement. Hon. gentlemen propose to run a road from Moncton away to the north of the height of land to Winnipeg and in that way they will create a north and south in this country. Any serious candid man will see the reasonableness of that proposition as opposed to the one the government propose. Are the lumbermen and the men who are interested in the timber of this country anxious to see a road run up there long before the timber that is there will be taken out and utilized ? There are millions of cords of wood between this and where you are proposing to go. It would do this country and the pulp business a great deal more good if hon. gentlemen would have the courage to put an export duty on pulp wood. An export duty on pulp wood would do more to develop that industry than three railways such as hon. gentlemen propose to build and yet, Sir, with one stroke of the pen the Finance Minister could bring that about, but he has not the courage to do it, nor has the government the courage to back him up. One stroke of the pen would do more to develop the pulp business of Canada than this railway will do. Put an export duty on pulp wood and what do you find ? Paper
mill after paper mill brought over into this country from the United States. Why ? Because Canada owns nearly all the pulp wood on this continent. Travelling through the country you will find agents of American large manufacturers of pulp wood machinery going into this country and building mills for Canadian people. One of these gentlemen said to me the other day, a man who has been in London putting in machinery for the Lloyds and men of that class, that if Canada put an export duty on pulp wood the American mills would move over to Canada. They could not do anything else. Why do not hon. gentlemen do something of that kind. They could save their $300,000,000 with one stroke of the pen and do Canada more good than all their proposition will do. But they dare not do that; they could not do that; that would be businesslike.
Before I sit down, I want to say that the government are obligating the country to an enormous outlay and are not solving the question. You would think to hear these gentlemen talk that there was no road now across this country. No way of getting down to a Canadian port. That is the only inference that can be drawn from what they say, that there is no outlet and there is no grain brought over a Canadian route. Who can say the traffic they talk about will go over the road they propose to build after it is built, and there is this to be said further that the western people must get to, the lakes, that is the important factor to them. Once they get to the lakes, competition will take care of the grain and we have the best waterway on the continent. Yet, Sir, hon. gentlemen do not realize the importance of making it any part of the grain route and the traffic route of this country. They are married to this scheme. They think that they will never have a name if they do not build this road. It is a question if they will ever have it, after they get through with it, but. I want to say this that they will realize before they are through that the difficulties in carrying out a proposition of this kind have not been provided for in the agreement submitted to the House. Who is going to run the road when you get it built ? Who is going to run the part you complete before the eastern section is completed ? The Grand Trunk Railway are not obliged to take it until it is all built, and I do not know if there is anything that will oblige them to take it then unless they think it is a paying scheme. The Grand Trunk Railway do not become responsible for the eastern end of the road and that is the important part to find responsibility for. The government are taking all the responsibility in reference to that and are giving the paying part, the part that will be able to take care of itself, up through the Peace River district one of the most fertile in this country, to the company.

Referring to what the leader of the government has said in reference to the wheat section of the country, it will he remembered that he traced the develpoment of wheat growing in this country, first on the St. Lawrence then in the Genessee valley, then Ohio, Illinois, Wisconsin and Dakota and now it has gone over from Dakota into Manitoba. Who ever dreamed of raising more grain than the United States? Who ever dreamed of raising more than the Americans ? He said it has left Minnesota and Dakota and gone to Manitoba and the reason for building this road is that the centre of wheat growing will leave Manitoba and go to the Peace river. What will Manitoba think of the fertility of her soil being exhausted in two or three years ? Surely the right hon. gentleman did not talk seriously. Yet that is what he said, it appears in ' Hansard,' and the wheat growing section of the country has moved over into Manitoba and it is surely going to move into the Peace river district ; hence the necessity of the road. Well, Manitoba will be raising wheat I think long after that road is built and her fertile soil will be still growing wheat when many changes will have come to pa^s in this country.
We cannot, for a moment, consider the condition of things in the west without Seeing the necessity of giving them an outlet to the lakes and then using the water-ways to the markets of the world. The ocean freight will largely control the route of the grain and that is what the government has not provided for, and I think that if they are going to make this scheme a success that is something that ought to be considered in the undertaking. There ought to be some obligation in reference to that. But I wish to show that the true solution of this question will not be accomplished at all even if this road is built. It will not lessen the shipping of grain by American ports one solitary cent, because it is only stipulated in that agreement that they will not charge more than somebody else charges. What does that give ? It gives to the company which carries the grain the alternative of going to the other place. We do not charge any more for going to Halifax than they charge for going to Portland- you can go to Portland. I do not see that any other construction can be put upon it. The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd) understood all about the contract last night, but that is something which I am afraid he has not looked into. The Minister of Justice will have to bring in a few more outside legal gentlemen to see what it means. He has already had to do it. It is evident that the Minister of Justice, in dealing with the question the other night, did not feel at home. It is easy to see that he did not get all he wanted in the agreement, and he did not like to talk about it. for fear he would make a mistake. I do not believe there is

one in the cabinet who got what he wanted. They got what the Grand Trunk would give them, that is all. G. M. Hays, as general manager of the Grand Trunk, just gave them what he thought the Grand Trunk could best get along with ; and now they are obliged to try to justify it. That is the position they are in, and they cannot get away from it. The Grand Trunk people would not touch the eastern division ; they would not sign any guarantee for it. They would only guarantee the part that was sure to pay. They have not a particle of responsibility for the eastern section. The government are going to build that, and hand it over to them, and maintain it for fifty years. Nobody knows what it will cost. The road will have to be run or go to the bad, and the government will have to face that responsibility. There is nothing to oblige the Grand Trunk Pacific to run that road, if I understand the agreement. Then, who is to run it V It is your road ; it is your capital that is put into it; all they agree to give you is a certain interest. Suppose they refuse to touch it, what recourse have you ? You can take what belongs to you; that is all the security you have got. It is like a man giving a mortgage on his own farm, and thinking he has made a splendid bargain. The Grand Trunk have a controlling interest in the stock, and will dictate to the Grand Trunk Pacific what they must do about this, that, and the other ; and you cannot help yourself. That is why they do not touch the eastern division. They feel safe with the western division, because it is going through a country that will develop rapidly, and will yield large receipts both for freight and passenger traffic. But that does not apply to the eastern division, which is going through a country where there is nothing but trees and lakes. Where is your traffic to come from ? The only traffic you can get is from the far west. But it is said that we will bring down a lot of timber by rail. The history of the past does not prove that you will bring the timber down by rail. You will bring it down the rivers, if you bring it down successfully and at the lowest cost. Then, where is your railway business to come from ? Logs are floated down the Ottawa river for hundreds of miles, and that is the cheapest way to bring them down. You can easily see why the lumbermen will not saw their lumber in the woods and bring it down by railway. They prefer to float the logs down the streams and saw them near the centres of population, where the haulage will be short. Then, this idea of the railway getting a large business from pulp wood is ail in the air. That is not the way the business will be developed. Your passenger traffic is not there, because, as I said before, no sensible man will travel from Winnipeg to Quebec and through Halifax on this road, when he can go on others

which will take him through the centre ot population. Then, your freight rates have to be higher, or your road will not pay.
Now, I have detained the House long enough ; but I wish to say, before I sit down, that I think the government ought to consider, and consider seriously, the question that is at the door of parliament seeking for solution-the question how to reduce freight rates most effectually. You cannot afford to pay fifteen or twenty cents a bushel to carry sixty cent wheat to market. If you want to encourage immigration to the North-west and make the people happy and contented, the way to do it is to give them lower freight rates. If you do not do that, you will have irritation, disaffection and trouble. This road will not do it, and 1 do not believe the government think it will. As the Premier said, it is not a commercial scheme, but a national scheme. The idea of building up a great nation has seized that gentleman, and they are going to run this road through, not in the interest of the country, not in the interest of the settlements now clamouring for relief, but in the interest of people whom they say they are going to send into the new country. The question has occurred to me whether the hon. gentlemen have the idea of bringing in some people from northern Europe, such as Finns and Norwegians, and settling them there. They do not pretend to say that they are going to settle that country with people from Ontario and Quebec ; and if they are going to such an enormous outlay, I suppose they are doing it with the intention of putting some people on the land along the line of the railway. The strongest advertisement that can be put out against this railway as a colonization road is the statement of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), that if you send a man to the North-west, he will get rich in five years, while if you keep him where he is he will be poor ail his life. So that, according to this statement, you are building this road to keep the people poor all their lives. I think the hon. gentleman's compatriots will resent that sort of treatment. We have built a railway into the Lake St. John district, yet it takes a good deal of trouble to keep the people there. They get tired of the place after they have been there a little while, and move out; and I think that the hon. gentlemen who are cognizant of the facts realize that the same difficulty will exist along the line of this railway ; the people will move out, and you cannot hinder them. The Lake St. John country, I understand is a good country. That country is not settled. The Lake St. John Railway has cost money. We have no less than seven roads running northward from the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway and other lines between Quebec and Lake Nepigon. My idea is that the proper system would be to push out these roads into the new country and let settlement go in from the present settlements northward, instead of running the line ns the government proposes. The question really before the country is the giving of cheaper transportation by means of utilizing our great waterways. We have a great waterway, intended by nature to be a thoroughfare between the east and the west, and, Sir, whatever scheme of transportation or development overlooks our interests in that respect, overlooks the real interests of the people of this country. You cannot solve that question if you ignore that great system of lakes waiting for the legitimate business that ought to cross it. Why can Chicago send grain around Lake Michigan to Buffalo and then carry it to New York, so much cheaper than we can ? We have a better route if we will only take care of it. The government took the tolls off the canals this year, which was good policy. We only got about $43,000 per year from these tolls, and what has been the result of taking them off ? The result has been that down the St. Lawrence this season over 7,000,000 bushels of grain went to Montreal, while less than 2,000,000 went to New York. That shows you how a very little lessening of the cost of traffic will affect the trade. If the government are anxious to lay out a lot of money anl control the outlay of millions of dollars, let them put the money they propose to expend on this road into a twenty-five foot waterway from the Georgian bay. That would not only give an outlet for the grain and other products of our great west, but the products and grain of the southwestern states as well. All the grain of the western country on the American side would come down our route. If you are anxious to lay out millions, there is a proposition which will give you some return for your outlay. I am opposed to the government handing over our waterways to any company. They ought to be held by the government in the interests of the people and developed along the line that would best suit the interests of the people generally. You can best settle this country east and west by making it the best country in the world to live in. But this proposition before the House will not solve the question. Neither the government nor its friends can say it does. What do they do ? They wave the flag. There is nobody in the country more pleased to see them loyal than I am. There never was anything they needed more, judging by their past ? Why, in 1891, they were willing to go right into the arms of the United States. The United States, they said, was the only natural market for this country, and the hon. gentleman who declared war the other day (Mr. Charlton) was the greatest advocate of that policy. But now they are the direst enemies of the United States. What was the reason they gave to the people, why the people should elect them at that time ? Their main rea-



sou was that because the Conservative party were not friendly with the American government, that party could not got anything from the Americans. But inasmuch as the Liberal party were the friends of the United States, they could get all kinds of good things from that country for Canada. Well, they have now been in power seven years and have not got anything. They went to Washington and came back as empty as they went. Consequently today they are declaring war upon that country. In my opinion the best thing we can do is to mind our own affairs and solve what questions come before us for solution with regard solely to Canadian interests. We have questions to solve which require a good deal of patient study, a good deal of research, a good deal of careful looking into before we can reach a proper solution. But these gentlemen rushed into this important undertaking without a moment's consideration or warning and cast it into the arena of public discussion. If there is one thing more than another which this government ought to do, but which they have not the courage to do, it is to appeal to the country on this scheme and get the verdict of the country upon it. They intend instead to send their friends around after the session to feel the pulse of the people, and if they think that pulse beats favourably, they will likely go to the country. But if the pulse does not beat just as they think it should, they will wait a little while longer. But they ought to have the courage of their convictions, and appeal to the country, and let the great tribune of the people decide whether or not this scheme is to the interests of Canada. I do not wish to detain the House further except to say, as a humble member of the Conservative party, I do not intend to take any lecture from the other side as to what kind of loyalty I sho lid have. Just think of hon. gentlemen opposite lecturing this side on the quality of loyalty. I am aware that new converts no always most enthusiastic, and I can ther store quite understand the strong enthusiasm which permeates the ranks of these new converts to the sentiment of loyalty to Canadian interests. But the people will be justified in watching them carefully. They remind me of a man who was cutting down a tree and was not sure of how it was going to fall. He came to me, about 150 rods away, and asked me to go with aim and shew him just which way it would drop.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are waiting to see which way the tree is going to fall. But it is not down yet. I do not propose to be lectured by that side as to my loyalty. We have had on this side to fight for the Canadian interests against hon. gentlemen opposite. We had to fight in the London market, the Grand Trunk Railway influence when we were financing to build the Canadian Pacific Railwmy. We had to fight the

influence of hon. gentlemen opposite on the London market as well, when they were decrying Canadian interests and declaring that' the Canadian Pacific Railway would never be a profitable undertaking. We had to fight all these influences before we could push the great Canadian Pacific Railway to completion and make the Dominion what it is to-day. These gentlemen climb on top of the House that Jack built. They think themselves very tall, as they stand there and say :	' Look at the house we have
made.' And if they were not on top of the house that Jack built, nobody would ever see them or know about them. The right lion. Prime Minister wants his name to go down to posterity linked with some great scheme as Sir John Macdonald's was linked with the Canadian Pacific Railway. He hopes that it will be Sir John Macdonald and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the Grand Trunk Pacific. Rut the hon. gentleman had better be careful how he carries out his idea. He does not know who is to own this road when it is completed. Who will it belong to, anyway ? The government cannot own it, for the road will cost $100,000,000 or more, and the Finance Minister -says that the only cost to the government will be about '$8,500,000, if I remember well, while the leader of the House says the cost to the government will be $13,000,000. It will hardly be pretended that the government can own the road when it pays so very little, and the Grand Trunk is not very likely to admit their claim. But does any man in Canada consider seriously this statement of the Prime Minister that the cost of this road to the country will be only $13,000,000 ? The right hon. gentleman says that we are only going to pay the interest on the money. But who is to pay for the bonds in fifty years ? If the calculation of the government is right and this road is going to cost the country only $13,000,000, then, there never were in public life men deserving of stronger condemnation. If they have the secret of building roads for one-eiglith of what they are worth, then, there should not be a square mile in Canada to-day which they had not provided with railway accommodation. They are going to get this road according to their story for less than one-eiglith of its cost
That is pretty cheap.

Very cheap. But if you get the goods at that rate you may be certain they are pretty poor. But nobody supposes tliat the right hon. Prime Minister is serious when he says that the expense to the country will be so small as this. Like myself he likes his little jokes once in a while, and this is one of his jokes. Otherwise, he has not been true to Canada in not using this secret of his to provide railways everywhere. Why, on the basis of the hon.

gentleman's figures our public debt really amounts to very little. Hon. gentlemen opposite went up and down the country for years talking about tbe rascally Tories increasing the public debt. Now we find there is nothing in it. for we only pay the interest on that debt. These hon. gentlemen are going to reduce the debt by $3,000,000, and they make a great deal out of that statement. But three millions, according to their figuring is only a few thousand, so they have nothing to brag about. When I was a boy at school I studied a certain kind of arithmetic. But these hon. gentlemen seem to have a new style. It has no multiplication table in it, and no addition-just subtraction. In the old Irish arithmetic of Foster & Goff that I studied, there was what was called the rule of false. You solved a problem by supposing something which was not so and working from that supposition. It seems to be that is how this road is going to be built. A man who knew the dark corners of Foster & Goff, in my early days was supposed to be able to do anything. It is evident that the government have studied the dark corners of Foster & Goff, and they are going to build this road on the basis of an arithmetic not known to most of us. Still, they are not able to tell us who will own the road when it is all done. I think they will find that the western end, which will pay, will belong to the Grand Trunk, and the eastern end, which will cost something to run, will belong to the government. The Grand Trunk does not touch your eastern end of the road at all-they have no responsibility for it. They know too much about railways for that. The ministers are under the impression that they know all about railways. They went to bed one night knowing nothing of the subject and they woke up next morning first rate railway men. Still, they cannot get Mr. Hays to have anything to do with the eastern end of this line. The right hon. leader will have the eastern end of the road as a monument to the folly of this House and of the government, if he does not look out. It is not going to pay, and I have already quoted what the hon. gentleman said in 1898 to the effect that the government should not touch anything that would not pay in a commercial sense. He does not pretend to say that this will pay, but tells us that it is not altogether a commercial, but a national undertaking. But I will not even give it that credit. It will be left as a national undertaking with the Dominion government simply because no one else would have anything to do with it. But the western section will pay its way right along, and the Grand Trunk will take that end of it.
I have spoken at greater length than I intended. In closing I merely express the hope that the government will consider the larger proposition that has been laid before parliament by the leader of the opposition, 295}
a proposition which will help to solve the question of cheapening freight rates for the people of the country, a thing which cannot be done by the policy of the government.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to say anything on this question until I heard my hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder) giving such awful descriptions of the route over which this road is to run. He spoke of mountains two thousand feet high and other obstacles just as great. I think, perhaps I can enlighten the hon. gentleman as to a portion of the route. As to the extreme eastern end, I do not pretend to know anything about that ; but as to the central portion, from Quebec to Winnipeg, I have been over a good deal of that country, and possibly I know a little more about it than almost any other member in this House. Well, I want to tell them that the height of land on this portion of the road is as level as it is on either side, or nearly so. There are no mountains or hills.
I did not say that it is not a level country along all the height of land, but that is where you will have to go to get a level country, it is not level outside of that.	.

There is no doubt that when this road leaves Quebec it starts off in a north-westerly direction, and it will not touch the height of land for 300 or 400 miles. I do not see any reason why it should cross the height of land until you get into Ontario, not in Quebec, because the country is as level there on one side as it is on the other. The member for Dundas says that people won't run railroads into that country for fear of setting fire and burning up the pine, and he wants to know if we are going to take pine timber out by railroad. I do not know what corner of the earth the hon. gentleman lives in if he has not seen timber coming down the Ottawa river here for the last thirty years and carried off by rail, millions of feet. I can tell him that there is a great quantity of pine in that country, part of it in Quebec, that we cannot get out in any other way.
Did not that timber largely come over the road owned by Mr. Booth, to his own mill ?

No, the hon. gentleman does not know what he is talking about. He will be safe in talking about woollens but not about lumber. Millions of feet of lumber have come down over the Canadian Pacific Railway from a region 200 or 300 miles on the other side of North Bay, and that is brought down and rafted from Ottawa. Now, Sir, we have heard it said that the country through which this road is to run from Winnipeg to Quebec is a worthless country. Well, I am well acquainted with the country on both sides of the height of land, for a length of 500 or 600 miles, and I can tell the hon. gentleman that it is not worth-

less. There is some of the finest pine grown there in the Dominion of Canada, on both sides of the height of land, especially on the south side. There is a large tract of country around Grand Lake Victoria, on the Ottawa river, containing thousands of miles of limits, and which cannot be got out except by railway. We have been trying to get a route by the Gatineau river to strike into that country and get a railroad built there, but we have never succeeded. When this new road goes in there I think it will touch a bay of that lake. The lake is forty or sixty miles long, very large and wide, and it has one bay that runs twenty miles north, right up to the height of land. I think it would pay well to strike that bay with this road, and if it does, there is pine enough in that country to keep that road running for ten years, giving it all it can do. There is as fine board pine there as ever went into the English market, and it must come out by railway. The country is a forest country, there is hardly any burnt land in. it. It is forest from 100 miles of Quebec, I suppose, away into Ontario about 300 miles. I venture to say that when that road is built there will be more sawmills along it than there are on the Ottawa river at the present time. There is tamarack, yellow birch and pine; in fact you will hardly find any part of that country on either side of the height of laud that has not pine, though perhaps not in as large quantities as we used to get out years ago.
The report of the Ontario surveyors says there is no white pine to speak of north of the height of land.

The report of the surveyors possibly refers to the Abitibi and Moose river regions, that is the route they all take. But I am talking about the bush, away in the interior where there are canoe routes beyond the lake. I do not think there is any pine in that country the surveyors speak of, but there are other large rivers that start from the height of land, and you do not have to go many miles before you reach large quantities of white pine. Talk about the engineers going into that country to find pine, I think the lumbermen, outside the Indians, know more about it than any other people in the world. I have travelled over that country myself, and I have paid thousands of dollars to explore it. We get reports from our buskmen; we keep bushmen travelling all the year round in that country. I have a report book at home that will show the character of the country north of Ontario and Quebec, showing whether it is level or rough, and the character of the forest. But of course that is private information. That is not to be given to the hon. gentleman. Each lumberman is supplied with a report showing where the best pine is, and on what river it is, but this information is not given out to the public. Hon. gentlemen might get information from some Mr. MACKIE.
lumbermen that would not cost them anything, but they could go there and locate the timber as well as I can. I think the lumbermen know more about the route this road is going to take than most of the engineers. You will hardly find a lumberman in the city of Ottawa that has not a report book dealing with some parts of that country.
We hear it reported that the land is no good, that it won't raise grain or anything else. Now, I have seen as fine potatoes, cabbage and turnips and all such things grown at Lake Abbittibbi as I have seen in any part of Ontario. That is near the boundary line between Quebec and Ontario. The boundary line is at Lake Abbittibbi, about 400 miles from Quebec. I am speaking of the country this side of the line, in Quebec. There are blocks of a thousand acres, or two or three hundred acres-it may be broken a little- of as fine land as there is anywhere within-500 miles of the city of Ottawa. I do not know but that it will raise as good crops, it may be a little far north for wheat. But Manitoba at one time did not raise good wheat, wheat used to get frozen there, but now it does not, and farmers understand better how to regulate their crops. But my intention was only to give a description of a part of this country that this road will run through, and I do not think that there is a better country in Canada for a railroad than a region 500 or 600 miles long that will be traversed. I do not see why there should be any fault found with a road being built there. It is a direct route from Quebec to Winnipeg, and you cannot get a more direct route. The idea of going away around by Toronto, and I suppose by North Bay, to get to Winnipeg-why, the thing is ridiculous. When you have such a country as that you want to open it up, and I think Ontario will get more benefit from this road than any other part of the country. That is a new country, the lumberman has never got back that far because it costs too much to get in supplies. It means taking them in with canoes in summer, and drawing them in winter over miles and miles of snow. Any man who has worked up there don't make much out of the run, because it costs too much to take in his supplies. This pine I speak of on Grand Lake Victoria, is about 200 miles above where any lumber has been cut.
Is that in the district of Nipissing or Algoma ?
It is in the Lake Abitibi district.
But I mean this Lake Victoria ?

I am not talking about the Nipissing district. I am talking about the route of this proposed railway. The district to which I am referring now is at the head of the Ottawa river. The railway will
9418

have to run parallel with the Ottawa river for about 200 miles until it crosses the boundary between Quebec and Ontario. That portion of the Ottawa river has never been improved and it is not likely that it will be, and the pine in that country will have to come out by rail. The square timber will be made with the axe and the logs will be sawed up there. The lumber will be taken out by rail. Lake Abitibi is near the watershed. It is on the canoe route to Hudson's bay. You cannot get any transportation by steamboat within about 300 miles of it. You have to go in your canoe, and that is the reason why that country is not settled. This railway will open up the region to which I refer. No branch railway can open it up as well as a through line, because the proposed line follows along the boundary and a country in which fine agricultural land is found. There is as good farming land on this side of Lake Abitibi, in the province of Quebec, as there is to be found in any portion of that province, and when you get across the boundary line into the province of Ontario you will find that settlers are located right up to the boundary line. The boundary line follows the Ottawa river until it gets to the head of Lake Tgmiscamingue, when it strikes due north towards James bay. Settlement on the Ontario side extends away northward along the boundary line, and there are some settlers near the height of land now. There are twenty good townships in that region that are filling up very rapidly. This road will go very close to these settlers, and the Tfimiscamingue Railway, which is being constructed by the Ontario government, will go right through the settlement, and the two will likely .loin at some point in that neighbourhood. I do not speak only from my own knowledge, but I base my statement also on the reports which we have received, that there is as fine land in the townships to which I have referred as there is in any part of Ontario. I am also told by the Indians and trappers that the land for 200 or 300 miles beyond is equally as good. This road is going to be a great benefit to the northern portions of Ontario and Quebec. I do not know of any other proposition that would confer as great a benefit upon this portion of the country. The government road running from North Bay will tap the transcontinental line somewhere in this vicinity, and there will be roads running from Port Arthur, from Quebec and other places, which will also connect with it, so that important centres south of the railway will have the benefit of branches connecting with the transcontinental line, which will also be an advantage to the settlements along the route of the road. As to the route below Quebec, I cannot say anything, as I do not know very much about that country. But I can tell the House one thing that surprises me, and it is the con-trat that the government have made with these railway people. I think it is all a
one-sided contract. I do not think there ever was a contract in Canada like it before.
Hear, hear.
It is all in favour of the people.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) was shouting before he was out of the bush. I think this scheme will confer a greater boon upon Canada than anything that any government has ever done. I know that some of the strongest supporters of hon. gentlemen opposite in their own counties have told me that if they oppose this road they need not go back for reelection. Of course, we do not expect some hon. gentlemen on the other side from western Ontario and around Toronto to do anything else. They will oppose any road that is not going into Toronto, or at least into Ontario. That is their general policy in this House. I think that some hon. members opposite from the province of Quebec, and especially the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), do not know anything about the north-west portion of their own province. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier does not think that that country has any value at all. I am surprised that an hon. gentleman who occupies the position of a leader; of his party should not know anything about his own province. I do not think he is qualified to represent the province of Quebec.
He may have obtained his information where the hon. gentleman did-from the Indians.

I do not need to go to the Indians or to any white man for any information that I have. I am, I think, well qualified to speak upon this subject. I have travelled through that country with my pack on my back and slept on three feet of snow every night. When you are travelling through that country it is impossible for you to tell when you have arrived at the height of land until you see which way the streams are running. If the streams are running northward, you know you are over the height of land. I do not want any hon. gentleman to tell me that this is not a good country to run a railway through. I never saw a better. Travelling on the Canadian Pacific Railway around the north shore of Lake Superior a man is in danger of his life going around those curves. I never want to go back to the North-west until there is another road built, and I think I will wait for this one, because this road will traverse a level country. Some hon. gentlemen have said that there are no water-powers on this route. There are the greatest water-powers on the Ottawa river not far from the proposed line of this road that I suppose there are any place in Canada. Of course, you cannot find water-powers byond the height

of land unless you go quite a distance from it. I do not see why this road should go beyond the height of land. I think it should be built on this side, because then it will open up a large tract of fine agricultural country- Any man who opposes this scheme who lives in Ontario is not doing Ontario justice, and I will say the same of any man living in the province of Quebec who adopts a similar course. There is no other proposition that can open up the country as advantageously as this. I hope that when the time comes some hon. gentlemen opposite will change their ideas a little. When I was in Quebec the other day I met a strong supporter of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), who asked me about this railway and who expressed the idea, strong Conservative as he is, that the hon. leader of the opposition should not oppose it. Possibly, when the vote comes that hon. gentleman will not be here, because we do not see him about very much. This railway will run through twenty-five or thirty townships of as good farming land as can be found in any part of the older province of Ontario, and it will open it up. I do not know that I have much more to say, except to express the hope that hon. gentlemen will consider the matter well before they rote.
