House went into committee on Bill (No. 147) to incorporate the Toronto and Hamilton Railway Company.-Mr. Campbell.
On section 11,

With regard to clause 11, I notice that the word ' communication,' an unusual word, is used there. Now that is certainly a word that is not common in Canada, and I would suggest that it should read ' or other public communication or place without first obtaining the consent.' That would make it quite clear. I do not know what a communication' is in regard to a street or anything else. It may have a significant meaning. I have no objection to using the words ' street or other public communication ' if the words ' or place ' are added after it. I cannot see any objection to that alteration, and it might happen that a square in the middle of a city or a park, might not be called a communication ; it would be a place, however.

I may say, that this Bill, as everybody knows, was very carefully considered in the Railway Committee for several days, and the amendments that were made to it were mutually agreed on by both parties and it went through the Mr. MACKIE.
committee unanimously, without any discussion, after this agreement. I do not like to see any changes made iu the Bill now, and I think so far as those two words are concerned. ' communication ' or ' place,' they mean identically the same thing. The word ' communication ' means, I suppose, a park, a square, a street, a highway. If you look at the dictionary yon will find that the word ' communication ' in this sense is derived from an old English phrase, and it means a place such as a park, a square, a street, a highway, where people communicate with oue another. I understand the object Mr. Barker has in view, that the city of Hamilton wants to take precautions that this railway shall not have the right to go through a park. Well, I think the word ' communication ' will fairly cover that, so that it cannot possibly do that, and any way there should be no objection to it, because under this clause, you will see that the railway has no right to run along any street or highway in any city or town without the consent of the municipality, and the municipality in giving their consent to run along any street or highway can easily stipulate that it shall not run through any park or any where else they choose. I have not had very much time to consult the promotors of the Bill, and I trust that my hon. friend will not press the alteration.

I quite admit all that the hon. gentleman has said. This Bill as it stands to-day was, as I understand, agreed upon at one o'clock in the morning, between the solicitors, but I have a duty to perform to my constituents, and I am not quite clear that notwithstanding the words 'public communication ' this railway company, if they get into the city of Hamilton, may not be able thereafter to run across two public parks in that city, which the citizens regard as so important that rather than have them interfered with they would keep this railway out altogether. I may mention that a short time ago a proposition was made to construct a railway from Galt into Hamilton, and the one point upon which the railway was prevented from going into Hamilton was that they wanted to run through the parks of the city, and get off the street. Now I understand the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell! to argue that ' communication ' does cover in the broadest, sense a public place. All I desire is to make it quite clear that a public place is included. I do not desire to force the question, unnecessarily, but it is an important matter to the citizens of Hamilton, and I submit that when the hon. gentleman says that the word ' communication ' will cover the word ' place ' he cannot have any objection to the words ' or place ' being inserted in the Bill, so that there may be no doubt about it. That is all I contend for, and I do not want to hamper the hon. gentleman now in his Bill in the least. Personally, I am opposed to the Bill from first to

last, but the Bill baying been agreed to I am content to allow it to pass. I want simply to add ' or other public communication or place,' that is public communication or public place. I have no objection to striking out the word ' communication,' but if they desire particularly to have that word in, I want to add the words ' or place,' and I do think the House will see the reasonableness of what I ask for. I would therefore, Mr. Chairman, move, that after the word ' communication ' in the third and sixth lines of clause 11, the words ' or place' be inserted.

I would suggest to the hon. member for Hamilton that as there is no difference of opinion as to what is desired and my contention is simply that the word ' communication ' covers all that is required. If my hon. friend thinks that it does not, I would suggest that you strike out the word ' communication ' and insert the word ' place ' in its stead.
I have no objection to that.

This is a new clause, which was not printed until to-day. I think this is the first time it has come into my hands. The first part of it reads, ' notwithstanding anything contained in the Railway Act.' Why should that not be, ' notwithstanding anything contained in this Act ' V It seems to me that the clause was wide enough to give the company the right to construct their line of railway along the highways under the General Railway Act without the consent of the municipality.

I was present in the committee when this alteration was discussed. I think that if the words, ' notwithstanding anything contained in the Railway Act,' were left out, the streets would be protected as against everything in this Bill. These words were inserted because some hon. gentleman in the committee thought that although this Bill might not permit the construction of a railway on the streets, the general Railway Act might do so.
I think there will be greater security by leaving the words in, otherwise there might be some clause in the Railway Act which, despite the words in the Bill, might allow a railway to come in.
The intention was to prevent any possibility of that.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended, agreed to.
On the question that the Bill be reported,

Before you report the Bill, I desire to say in the House what I said in the Railway Committee upon the subject of this Bill. I consider that this Bill is totally outside the jurisdiction of this
parliament. I have not opposed it in the House, because it was assented to by the parties immediately concerned on both sides. They, in good faith, as between themselves, agreed upon the clauses of the Bill; and although perhaps my objection and my voting against the Bill may be somewhat inconsistent, I desire to repeat here what I said in the committee, that I do not think this parliament has any power to pass this Bill at all. My motive for stating this in the House is this. One of the legal gentlemen who acted for the promoters of this Bill said, when the Bill passed the Railway Committee, that if the municipalities were unreasonable in refusing the permission under clause 11, it might be necessary for them to come back to the committee. In view of that statement of the counsel who was acting for the promoters of the Bill, I desire to say that I protest, and strongly protest, against such measures as this as an infringement upon provincial rights. I think it is wrong, extremely wrong, for this parliament to assume jurisdiction, contrary to the terms of the constitution under which we sit here ; and whenever such a Bill as this comes up,
I will always vote against it, as I would desire to vote against this Bill. I do not know that I need say anything more. I simply make this statement now to protect. myself, and I think to protect other gentlemen, perhaps on both sides of this House, who are opposed to such legislation as this, against the idea going forth that by passing this Bill any precedent is created under which other Bills of a similar character can be brought forward. I think it is necessary to say this, and to say it very emphatically, because all through the discussions of this Bill in the Railway Committee, we were met at every step by statements that similar Bills had already been passed by this House. For my part, I am not going to sit silent here and allow without protest a Bill to pass which may hereafter be brought forward as a precedent to authorize similar legislation in the future. I am very glad to be able to say here that in what I assert I have been endorsed, and very strongly endorsed, by the acting Minister of Railways and Canals, who expresses substantially the same view.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman why this Bill conflicts with provincial rights. He has not made that very clear.

1 have simply entered my protest. I do not wish to occupy the time of this House in re-discussing a principle which has already been fully discussed. When the measure was up on a previous occasion I went into that question, stating my reasons for believing that this measure does not come within the functions of this House, and I do not think it neces-

sary to occupy the time of the House or ' Hansard ' in repeating what I then said.

There is one observation of the hon. gentleman which I think perhaps he did not mean. I do not suppose the hon. gentleman intended us to understand that he thinks this measure is beyond the power of this House ?

I think it is beyond the power of this House, for this reason, that we state in this Bill a fact to give us jurisdiction, which fact I believe is contrary to the opinion of every hon. gentleman in the House.
Does the hon. gentleman mean that any court would hold that this Bill is ultra vires ?
No, I believe not, it would be precluded from so holding, by our misstatement of the fact.

That was my only purpose in asking the question ; because the hon. gentleman's statement was beyond what he really intended. On the main question, I entirely agree with the hon. gentleman, that we ought to have that fact proved in a general way to the satisfaction of any committee of this House before we assume jurisdiction over purely local and provincial jnatters. As far as the general principle is concerned, I wish to express my agreement with it.

X quite agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell). He has stated the legal position, I think accurately. I have no doubt whatever in my mind that if this House chooses to state as a positive fact in a Bill that a work is for the general advanage of Canada, there is no remedy- it follows, from the statement of the fact, solemnly made by the parliament of Canada, that the work is for the general advantage of Canada, that the Bill relating to it comes within our jurisdiction. But what I contend for is this, that when those words are used as a merejpretense, when there is no possible foundation for the state ment, we have no more moral right, sitting in this House, to enact such a measure, than we would have for supporting a Bill to authorize the construction of a village pound because we should choose to state that such a pound was for the general advantage of Canada.

I just wish to emphasize what the hon. member for Hamilton has said, by remarking, that there have been a great many measures similar to this passed through the Railway Committee and the House. The abuse, if I may use that expression without giving offence, of the privileges of this House has been carried to such an extent that the municipalities Mr. BARKER.
have had to make a very special and very strong appeal to the sense of justice and fair play of members of this parliament to stop this class of legislation. With the cooperation of hon. gentlemen on both sides, this measure has been shorn of its most objectionable features. As the hon. member for Hamilton has said, a compromise was reached which we are bound to stand by, but I hope that this will be the last Bill of this kind which will ever be presented to a Dominion parliament. This is an invasion undoubtedly of provincial and municipal rights. The intention of the promoters in coming here was to evade the obligations which would have been imposed upon them had they applied to the Ontario legislature.

While I agree in much that has been said, I would not like to say that a special case could not be made out. The general principle is correct, but I can understand, for example, that in the case of a city which a railway crossed and recrossed, a great continental line, it might be necessary that we should assume jurisdiction in the interest of the travelling public.

I am sure that my hon. friend, the senior member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), when he spoke of the practice of passing Bills by this parliament, which were of a provincial character, had no reference to this particular parliament or to any particular session, but to the Dominion parliament, speaking in the broadest sense of the word.
Hear, hear.

I well remember, as far back as twenty years, when this abuse of the British North America Act began ; and year after year since then, measures have been passed through the Dominion parliament which should have been dealt with by a provincial legislature. This was done by declaring such measures to be for the general advantage iof Canada when they really were not. On many an occasion, in days gone by, X have protested against this practice. I raised the same protest which has been raised in this case by the hon. member for Hamilton and others. It is well that parliament has been brought face to face with the situation resulting from this lax system of legislation. It is well that this measure has been thoroughly discussed in the Railway Committee, as we have thereby arrived at a clear idea as to how similar applications should be treated in the future. I would not venture to lay down a rule, but it seems to me that if I had to determine the policy and practice of the Railway Committee in a question of this kind, I would think it proper, if we are to give a fair interpretation to the British North America Act, that we should, in the first place, assume that every work which

is within tbe confines of a province is prima facie subject to the jurisdiction of that province only, and let the onus rest on those who seek to obtain legislation here to prove that the work is properly the subject of Dominion legislation. Unless they can establish that point clearly, the committee should not proceed to deliver judgment and give a federal charter to a work which it does not possess. This debate will not prove unprofitable if it results in educating members to the consequences of continuing the practice which has so long prevailed. As has been remarked, where are you to stop, if you are to declare, without inquiry or reflection, that any work that may be in existence in any nook or corner, municipality or parish, of this broad Dominion, is a work for the general advantage of Canada, and thus remove it from the jurisdiction of the local legislature, which ought to deal with it. Although this measure may become law, I venture to say that it will be many a year before parliament will be asked to pass legislation of a similar character.

No doubt whatever that the clause of the British North America Act has been given a scope it was never intended to have. It has been used over and over again, as a matter of course so that a declaration is made more as a matter of form than anything else, and I am inclined to think that probably it will be good policy for this parliament in the future to insist that any measure of this kind, by which it is intended to bring within the jurisdiction of this parliament an undertaking which is prima facie within the scope of provincial jurisdiction, should be either referred to a; select committee of the House, in order that the question of a fact may be absolutely proved, or be submitted to the determination of some judicial authority. There are of course many cases in which parliament itself would be the best judge. The Railway Committee or the Committee on Private Bills possibly might be the best judge. Those promoting the undertaking should be put into the position in which the promoters of private Bills in England are placed. If I understand the practice there, it is practically a judicial inquiry and a judicial determination upon important questions of fact involved in the preamble of the Bill. They are very much more strict than we are in such matters, and so far as this particular question is concerned, it would be very desirable that in the future we should adopt some such principle with regard to measures of this kind.

It is interesting, after the lapse of many years, to see parliament coming back to what was the intention of the framers of the British North America Act. I remember away back in 1879-80-82
and 1883, when the French Canadian members in this House were the only parties who objected to our legislative interference with what are undoubtedly the rights of the provinces. I remember very distinctly men who were regarded as eminent lawyers giving their opinion in the Railway Committee to the effect that although the declaration be made that the work is for the general advantage of Canada, unless the other conditions existed which brought it within the legislative authority of the federal parliament, it would not be hel'd by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council to be such a work. I have often regretted that these discussions did not take place in the House instead of in committee, as we then would have had a record of the debates. But I remember distinctly Mr. Hector Cameron and Mr. MacMaster, of Montreal, and several other prominent legal authorities, and Sir Hector Langevin as well, frequently expressing the opinion that we could not bring a work within the legislative jurisdiction of the federal parliament by the simple statement that it was for the general advantage of Canada, and that if the question came before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council it would so decide.
It seems that since that decision has been given which leaves the impression that a declaration in the Bill that the work referred to is for the general advantage of Canada, of itself brings the subject within the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament. What I think ought to have been done with a great many of these Bills is to submit the question to the Supreme Court. This is one of the objects for which the Supreme Court was established-to advise parliament on these questions of jurisdiction as between the provinces and the Dominion. A case could be stated at any time and submitted to the Supreme Court. We should have at least the advantage of their judgment, and if it was deemed advisable to carry the case further, that could be done. But it seems that we are getting back to where we were twenty years ago, with the added difficulty that this decision has been given which seems to show that the mere declaration, in a Bill, as I have said, brings the subject within the jurisdiction of this parliament. But. because of this very fact, it is all the more necessary that we should surround these measures with safeguards that will secure to the provinces the right of control over provincial corporations. When we deal with Bills relating to works that extend beyond the bounds of one province or with corporations that have rights or interests in more than one province. there may be some justification for our dealing with them. But surely a short electric railway, even though it may cross lines of railway which are within our jurisdiction, can hardly be fairly called a work for the general advantage of Canada

and so removed from provincial to federal jurisdiction.

The discussion is very interesting, and I think, very important. I do not go quite so far as to say that Bills of this kind should be referred to the Supreme Court, or to a judge of that Court. I am afraid it would interfere with the practical working of parliament.
But we have done it before.

I know it. But I doubt if we could do it in all these cases. But I would suggest that in all cases where a Bill contains a declaration that the work is a work for the general advantage of Canada, there should be a report from the government or from the Minister of Justice to the committee having charge of the Bill, giving the opinion of the government or of that minister, as to the propriety of the declaration in regard to the particular work dealt with in the Bill. That would not preclude the committee from deciding the question, but it would put upon the government of the day the responsibility of saying whether they thought parliament had jurisdiction in the matter or not. I believe that if the present government had had this question referred to them under such a rule, they would have reported to the Railway Committee that the work referred to in the Bill was not one for the general advantage of Canada. The subject was brought before a committee of the government and they heard statements of counsel representing the province of Ontario and other provinces. But tlie government saw fit to refer the matter back to the Railway Committee. Considering that such matters affect the working of our constitution, the committee should have the benefit of an opinion from the government or the Minister of Justice, stating whether on the face of it the Bill appears to be one providing for works which are within the juridietion of this parliament. I would not desire for a moment that tlie Railway Committee should be debarred from the right to discuss or decide upon tlie question. But I do think the committee should have the opinion of the minister for their guidance. And I feel fairly certain that if such protection were afforded to the public we should have very little trouble on the score of such Bills as this. I doubt whether a government representing either political party would report that the work referred to in this Bill was a work for the general advantage of Canada.
Mr. HEYI). I think we ought to go even a little further than the suggestion of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker). There should be certain conditions agreed upon that a railway company must comply with before it could be declared a work for Mr. SPROULE.
tlie general advantage of Canada. The conditions should work automatically, and not. be left to a majority of the Railway Committee, for that majority is always uncertain. The meaning of this phrase ' work for the general advantage of Canada ' should be declared so that a railway company, before it even aspires to be clothed witli tlie powers vested in these magical words, it should have to comply with certain conditions. Tlie effect would be to relieve the committee of a great deal of unnecessary work. It seems to me that the practice has insensibly grown up in the Railway Committee of granting the benefit of these words to railways that were not really entitled to use them. And many members did not know what the effect of the words was. I have asked in tlie House and in the Railway Committee what advantage accrued to a railway company to which these words applied, and no one has been able to tell me. The impression has gone abroad that an attempt has been made in this House to take from the provinces rights that belong to them. I am sure that no such desire exists on the part of any hon. members of this House. If we have erred in the past in granting to companies the privilege of having their works called works for the general advantage of Canada, it lias not been with tlie intention of robbing the provinces of any right belonging to them. If my suggestion were adopted and the conditions defined, our work of legislation would be done more smoothly and consistently. It should not be left to the majority of the Railway Committee in this general fashion to say whether a work is or is not a work for the general advantage of Canada. A majority of the Railway Committee might be friendly to one promoter, and declare the work he represented to be for the general advantage of Canada, while refusing the privilege to another equally entitled to it. We should define what those words mean, so that railways will be obliged to comply with the conditions laid down, and, complying with these conditions, they would be entitled to be called works for the general advantage of Canada.

With reference to the suggestion of the h n. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) that a clause of this kind should be subject to report from the government, I hardly think that, on reflection, the hon. gentleman will adhere to that view. The question that lies at the very threshold of the inquiry in each of these cases is one of facts, and parliament is the proper tribunal to inquire into that question of facts, either directly or by such machinery as it may invoke. When the facts are known, it is for parliament to apply the legal consequences by either bringing the work under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada or refusing to do so. But I would not favour parliament abnegating its functions to any govern-

ment or committee. It should retain the right to deal with those questions in its own way. Difficulty has arisen in the past because

The hon. gentleman totally misunderstood my suggestion. 1 did uot'suggest that the government should have the power to prevent parliament dealing with the question. I only said that when such a statement was made in a Bill coming before the Railway Committee, the Minister of Justice or some other minister should send a report to the committee for their information, stating that in his opinion he considered that work to come within our jurisdiction, that is to say, that it was a work for the general advantage of Canada. But I said moreover that I would not propose to preclude the Railway Committee or the House from deciding upon the question;
I only proposed that the committee and the House should have the advantage of the ministry speaking with the responsibility of a ministry upon that question.

I quite understood the hon. gentleman. My view is that the first inquiry is to ascertain what are the facts. Are the facts such as to warrant the statement, not within the meaning of the British North America Act in the first place, but to warrant the statement in the ordinary acceptation of the words that the work is of such general importance as to warrant its being removed from the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature and being brought under the jurisdiction of the Dominion parliament. That is a question of fact in the first instance, and I do not think that the Minister of Justice is any better qualified to pronounce upon this question of fact than any other member of parliament.
I was going to say that in my opinion parliament should not allow this procedure to be hampered or interfered with by a report of a government or by a report of any tribunal that is not appointed by this House.
I quite agree.

The government is after all no better able to judge of the facts than any .dozen members of this House. But I was going to make a suggestion, seeing that we are all seeking to accomplish the same end and to make suggestions that may hereafter bear fruit and cause proper consideration to be given to this point in connection with all other applications. I have not taken the opinion of my colleagues on this point. I merely give it offhand, the same as other lion, gentlemen are giving their views I presume. 1 was going to say that there are a number of rules in the standing rules of this House governing the procedure before Railway Committees, and it seems to me that the House itself might fairly formulate a rule dealing with a question of this kind, providing that when a Bill of this kind came
before the committee the first step to be taken should be to make the proper inquiry, leaving it with the committee of course to take such steps as it saw fit. But I think that some good would come by having one of the rules of this House provide for dealing with such cases in the future.
Mr. CLARKE There is another suggestion that might be made, and' it is that when legislation of this kind is being sought for which affects the rights and interests of great urban municipalities, it should be a prerequisite of such application before being considered by the proper committee, that the municipality to be affected should be specially notified that such legislation was being promoted, and the municipality should also be notified in what way its rights might be affected by legislation passed by this House as compared with provincial legislation.
A rule of the House might cover that.

In this connection I may say that the city of Toronto has spent three quarters of a million dollars on what is known as the Don improvement. The work was constructed by the city, with the sanction of the legislative assembly. It was practically a local improvement work, but by some means it has been declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, and the city of Toronto is getting a rental of $750 a year for that enormours expenditure. Muneipalities whose rights have been invaded by legislation of this kind are naturally suspicious, and I think if the onus of responsibility were thrown upon promoters of notifying municipalities that were likely to be affected by proposed legislation, additional safeguards for the rights of municipalities would be afforded which do not exist at the present time.

On Monday next the House will be called upon to consider the report of the select committee ou the rules of the House. It would be out of order for me now to refer to those rules further than to say that one of the proposed rules is that in connection with an application of a telegraph or telephone company for legislation, in addition to the notice being published in the ' Canada Gazette,' a similar notice should be published in some leading newspapers. Perhaps that might not altogether meet the case, perhaps the notice, instead of appearing only in the 'Canada Gazette' and one other paper, should be published in the papers of the locality to be affected by the proposed legislation. If that does not go far enough, perhaps my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) would consider this suggestion, and when this Bill comes before us on Monday next, he would suggest something of the nature he has mentioned, for example, an additional notice.
A specific notice to the clerk of the municipality.
This would afford a good opportunity, at all events, to discuss that point.

We must remember that a work that may now be considered for the general advantage of Canada, ten years hereafter may not be so considered, because new circumstances will arise. I would not wish to be bound by a rule made even by the wisest House that ever sat in Canada, as to any particular work being for the general advantage of Canada. You must leave that to the evolution that takes place in'all countries and societies. Growing as we are, each succeeding parliament will be called upon to deal with the facts as they then exist. You cannot deal on hand and fast lines with a clause like this, because year after year and decade after decade circumstances will change.
Motion agreed to. Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
