speakeroldname: Mr. J. R. LA YELL (Leeds and Grenville).
speechtext: We have bad the pleasure of listening to the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Mac-kie), who gave us his opinions on this Bill, which of course be is entitled to do, as is every other member of this House, but his opinions can only have weight according to the weight of the reasons that he alleges in support of them. We have also heard from him certain statements which we may speak of as statements of fact and which were of interest to the members of this House. Among other statements made by the hon. member was that he knew more of that country through which this road from Winnipeg to Quebec is to pass than any other hon. member of this House. I presume, in making that statement, he also included the right hon. leader of the government. He then proceeded to tell us what lie knew. I sincerely trust that much of the northern portion of Ontario, as also of Quebec, is of the quality which he describes but we have to confine ourselves to the country that he specially knows and not give weight to any opinion he may form. He tells us that he has gone through the north country, that he has seen the height of land, that he lias crossed it and that he has examined

the country on both sides of it. For what distance has he examined it ? He tells us that he has knowledge of it for 400 or 500 miles and he also tells us that he has personal knowledge of it for 100 miles.
I did not say that. I said I had personal knowledge of it for 100 miles in Ontario.
Very well. The hon. gentleman has personal knowledge of it for one hundred miles in Ontario, and also, I presume, he has personal knowledge for 300 miles in Quebec ?
Yes.

That is personal knowledge of 400 miles of country in all. This railway covers a distance from Winnipeg to to Quebec of a little over 1,400 miles in a straight line, not an air-line, because it is impossible to build an air-line. That, I think has to be admitted. The most optimistic speaker on this proposition, the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) added 10 per cent to the distance to find out how much farther the road would have to go. The least distance was 1,500 miles, according to his estimate. His estimate is altogether too small, because I think it would be easily ascertained that no railway between points in eastern Canada has even been built within a distance of 10 per cent more than the air-line. Not long ago the Canadian Pacific Railway in building a piece of line without a subsidy and desiring to get the shortest possible distance between Perth and Toronto, built the line as straight as it could, but it did not succeed in keeping it within 15 per cent of the airline. When you add the percentage of additional distance that it would be necessary to build in connection with this proposed new line, the mileage will be more nearly 1,500 or 1,600 miles than 1,400 miles between Winnipeg and Quebec. The hon. member has been over some 400 miles of this distance. He admits that he does not know the location of the line and he has only knowledge or professes to have information of less than one-quarter of the distance to be covered by the line as to its fertility and resources. There are others who have crossed the height of land and there are various heights of land that have to be crossed all over this country. It has been noticeable that the height of land is generally level, but that by no means proves that the height of land is fertile. I know that in the days when I could find time to go on long canoe trips, I had the pleasure to cross the height of land some distance north of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I admit that the height of land was level, I admit that it was very difficult to tell even when you came to the height of land, save by the waters flowing each way, but even the imagination of the hon. member for North Norfolk could not conjure up any fertility

in that region. Of course, I was simply hunting for scenery. The hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Maclde) was hunting for lumber. We probably both found what we were seeking. This shows the singularly small amount of information which we have concerning that region, and the possibility of building a railway through it. I will probably touch upon that again.
Notwithstanding all that has been said upon this question, it is necessary either in starting to criticise it or in expressing the opinions of an hon. member of this House on it to review the proposition even although it has been already done. There is a story told about a certain lawyer in one of our courts of appeal. He had been defeated in the court below, and having appealed to a higher court, he commenced to lay down some elementary principles when the chief justice interrupted him and asked him if he would not give the court credit for knowing something about the primary principles of law. His answer was this : That is just the mistake I made in the court below, my lord. X think from the way in which hon. gentlemen opposite have carefully avoided some of the principal facts in connection with this whole transaction, that they should be repeated very often, for after all, we have to come down to some preliminary principles which ought to be put forth in connection with any such proposition as that which is now before the House. What is the proposition ? It is one that involves, as the right hon. leader of the government said, two principles, one the granting of a charter to the Grand Trunk Padflc Railway Company to build a road from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean, and in connection with that road to give a guarantee and a certain amount of cash subsidy for that is what the payment of interest on the bonds for a number of years means, and the other part of the proposition is that the government shall build the road itself from Winnipeg to Moncton via. Quebec, and having built it hand it over to the Grand Trunk Pacific. That is the proposition in short subject to the details as they will be found in the agreement attached to the Bill. What is the reason given for the building of this road ? We have in this House heard , as many different reasons as there have been different speakers on the government side. But, I presume that we may give the right hon. leader of the government credit for knowing the reason for the faith that is in him better than any of his followers, and he has given practically three reasons. I am going to quote from his own words the reasons given by him upon introducing this Bill. He said that this work is undertaken, this contract is made :
To provide immediate means whereby the products of these new settlers may find an exit to the ocean at the least possible cost.
He is referring to the new settlers in
Manitoba, the North-west and British Columbia. Then, here is his second reason :
Whereby, likewise, a market may be found for those who toil in the forests, in the fields, in the mines, in the shops of the older provinces.
It is well to look again at this second reason, and to follow the elaboration of the right hon. gentleman. He is referring to these settlers pouring into the North-west Territories in countless numbers, thousands and hundreds of thousands, he has mentioned, and he says that for one, two or three generationls, the new settlers will grow cereals and probably nothing else. He proceeds :
They will have need of everything that is required by civilized men. They will have need of clothing, furniture and every , kind of manufacture. Then, Sir, what shall we do ? Shall we allow them to be supplied by our American neighbours, or shall we provide a railway which shall enable our manufacturers in Ontario and Quebec to supply them with what they shall require ?
I would ask the House to bear in mind these two main, reasons, although there is another and very important reason given by the right hon. gentleman :
These are the two main reasons for building the road. There is a third which I will deal *with more fully and dispose of before touching on these two reasons.
And that third was the need of being independent of bonding privileges. Now, Sir, this is the argument of the right hon. gentleman that has been carefully analysed already by the ex-Minister of Railways, and has been referred to repeatedly by different speakers who touched on this matter. Attention has been drawn to the way in which the right hon. gentleman dealt with this matler. I might read his words. They are worthy of repetition. In speaking with regard to this bonding privilege, of our position with regard to the United States, and of the necessity of our being commercially independent of the United States, he says :
What is our position to-day ?
He does not say what was our position a good many years ago, but ' What is our position to-day ? '
What is our position to-day ? Prom the early days of railway development of this country, we have been dependent on American good-will for the transportation of our goods across American territory. From the early days of Canadian railway development, we have been forced to make use of American territory and harbours.
He repeated almost this same language further in his address. He says :
If we have used American ports and the bonding privilege it w-as not because our harbours were ice-hound in "winter but simply because we have no railways of our own to reach them.
Now, notwithstanding the fact that the fullest prominence has been given to the
943,

error made by the hon. gentleman in that, and that not only to-day, but for many years, we have had not only one, but two railways that connect with the harbours on the Atlantic coast ; notwithstanding this, that statement has been repeated over and over again. Surely, Sir, any school boy attending at any of our schools who went up to a departmental examination and gave such an answer as that when asked about our railway connections, would be, and most certainly would deserve to be plucked. It should be something well within the knowledge of every member of this House and of every citizen of this country that not long ago the exportation of cattle through the United States from certain parts of the interior was stopped. The Canadian Pacific Railway could not carry them across to St, John, because it would have to go through the state of Maine, and the Grand Trunk Railway could not carry them to Portland, and they were carried around hy the Intercolonial Railway ; and not only have we the Intercolonial Railway, but, as has been repeatedly referred to, we have another route by Edmundston connecting with the Intercolonial Railway for St. John. I emphasize this, not to call attention to the particular mistake, but to call attention to the fact that that simply illustrated the vagueness of detail and of knowledge of fact on which this whole project is based. There is a lack of exactness which augurs very ill for the successful carrying out of such a gigantic undertaking. That lack of exactness and the vagueness is not only illustrated by the statements made with regard to the bonding privileges, but it is further illustrated by what is proposed to overcome this difficulty. The member for Bonaven-ture (Mr. Marcil), referring to the need of our having an all-Canadian line, said the Intercolonial Railway had been built without regard to commercial principles, and was 300 miles too long. We have heard some pretty wild statements, but I think that is the largest estimate of the excess of distance of the Intercolonial Railway that has been made in this House. Well, that is one estimate, but we have on the other side the estimate of the ex-Mlnister of Railways, who said that 63 miles could be saved in a distance of several hundreds. We have further the estimate made by the right hon. gentleman who moved the resolution. He says that 120 to 140 miles can be saved-at least he says that in one part of his speech.
I have said that these estimates of the distance by which this proposed new railway might shorten the road between Quebec and Moncton, or Montreal and Moncton, were very vague, that the figures presented disagreed, but it is not simply the different speakers that disagree. We find in the speech of the right hon. gentleman when he was moving this Bill three different statements of the distance that could be saved. When he first refers to it he says :

If the truth must be told it must be said that those who conceived and carried out the Intercolonial Railway added to its length, to its normal length several hundred miles.
That is the first statement. The next statement is that it being necessary to make the shortest possible line, a line will have to be made going direct to Edmundston, close around the north of the state of Maine and from there to Moncton. That is the shortest possible way of making an allCanadian line. By doing this we can shorten the distance between Moncton and LSvis by from 120 to 140 miles. I might suggest that that is very different from several hundred miles, but probably it is just as clear as most of the facts that we have in connection with this new road. However, the right hon. gentleman desired to give a reason for the faith that was in him, and he referred to the knowledge that we had, and after speaking of knowledge that had been gained by lumbermen, by early explorers and others, he said that we have an exact survey, a survey of this very country that had been made under the government of Sir John A. Macdonald. He quotes from this the report of the engineer in charge, Mr. Davey, and this is the only exact report that is quoted by the right hon. gentleman, or that has been quoted by any member of this House. I am not going to quote that this session but at the close of this report Mr. Davy, according to the quotation made by the right hon. the Premier, says that the survey made by him showed that the distance from Montreal to Moncton could be shortened to 759 miles, but he said there was one place where 100 miles more could be taken off, and the total length from Edmundston to Moncton be reduced to 199 miles, which makes 749 miles from Montreal to Halifax. According to the time-table of the Intercolonial Railway, which is the only authority I have had an opportunity of consulting since reading that, it seems that the present line from Halifax to Montreal is only 87 miles more than that, so we find in the speech of the right hon. Premier three separate estimates of the distance by which the line from Moncton to Montreal may be shortened. The first is several hundreds, the next 120 to 140, and then when he comes down to read an engineering report, he is not larger than 87 miles. Well, that report is on paper, and is still a report, the line has to be built, and engineering difficulties always arise, and no one ever yet knew of a line being built in quite as short a mileage as the original estimate of the first engineer who went over it. I think we can take it for granted that the statement of the hon. the ex-minister of Railways was correct when he said that 63 miles is probably the very utmost by which the line between Montreal and Moncton, or Quebec and Moncton, can be shortened.
And it is for the sake of gaining 63 miles,

or let us say 87 miles, out of some 830, that this project of building a new line from Quebec to Moncton and then handing it over to a rival company, is to be undertaken. The cutting off of these 87 miles or less is to be undertaken, it is said with great gusto by the right bon. the Premier, for the sake of relieving us from the bondage of the bonding privilege. Well, that is worth examining. Suppose the United States did cut off its nose to spite its face ; suppose it did injure its own railroads and ports for the sake of causing injury to our Canadian railroads-because that is after all the meaning of it-what would be the result ? Of course, it would mean that Canadian goods for export would have to go around the north of the state of Maine. That question is settled, and rightly enough. As all who have examined the map know, that would be a most expensive route ; but what will be the best route ? The right lion, gentleman says that the route proposed by this Bill will be the shortest and the best. But this route would be considerably longer than the Canadian Pacific Railway short line to St. John or the Grand Trunk line to Portland ; consequently the haul over it would be more expensive per mile, and therefore it would be a more expensive route. But in the event of our railroads being attacked by means of any such hostile act as the repeal of the bonding privilege, who might better In the interests of Canada own this short route from Quebec to St. John or Halifax ? Would it not be infinitely better as has been suggested by the hon. leader of the opposition, that if that route needs to be built as a better and shorter route, that it should remain in the hands of the people of Canada ? Would it not be infinitely better that it should remain not only owned by the Dominion, but operated by the Dominion, so that in the event of such an act of hostility, the Dominion, if necessary, would be willing to lose a certain amount of money in order that our commercial interests should not be injured ? If necessary we could make it haul from Montreal or Quebec to St. John or Halifax at as low a rate as any of the railways of the United States offer to their seaports. The country could well afford to do that in order that our commercial interests would not be imperilled; but could we compel a private corporation to do that ? No legislation under the sun could compel private corporations to carry freight at a loss, though the country could afford to do it to meet that special emergency. If the proposed railway can get us out of the difficulty of the bonding privilege, it only shows that it should remain in the possession of and under the control of the government in order to serve the interests of Canada as a whole in the event of such a contingency.
There is another thing which, although attention has been called to it before, is
worth repeating. If this contract is carried out, and that road is built, it must of necessity be built to the injury of the Intercolonial Railway. That matter has heeu treated so exhaustively by the hon. ex-Miu-ister of Railways and Canals, that I do not propose to go into it; but I do desire to answer a somewhat serious proposition made by the hon. Minister of Finance. He asked how the building and running of this road would hurt the Intercolonial Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway, he said, had built a short line to Montreal, the Canada Atlantic, did not object to it, and the two roads are running. It seemed to me that the hon. Minister of Finance must have laughed up his sleeve when he said that. He must know that the two cases are not in the slightest degree parallel. In the first place, the two roads run through a populous district between two large centres of business. It would have been a closer parallel if when the proposition was mooted that the Canadian Pacific Railway should build a short line to Montreal, the Canada Atlantic Company had offered to build the line, had entered into a guarantee to see that it was kept up to date, and at its completion handed it over to the Canadian Pacific Railway on condition that after a few years the Canadian Pacific Railway would pay a small percentage for its use. That, I admit, is an insane proposition ; but it is hardly less insane than the proposition of the government to enter into a contract with a private company to build a better road than it has at present, and at the end of a certain number of years to hand it over to that private company for an annual payment of 3 per cent on the cost, without taking any guarantee that the road would ever be paid for. So much for the bonding privilege, which has been dealt with pretty freely by others.
The right bon. the Premier said that this new road would form an exit for the products of Manitoba and the North-west Territories to the ocean at the least cost. What exit is there now ? One would almost imagine from the speech of the right hon. gentleman that there is no exit now, but that the farmer of the North-west grows his crop and piles up his grain, and leaves it there until some one with a dray comes along and takes it out, or until settlement grows up in the neighbourhood large enough to consume it all. We have at present, I think, some means of getting our crops out of the North-west. I should imagine that our Trade and Navigation returns would prove that. How do they come out? It seems ridiculous to have to state it; but, from the speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite, it seems to be necessary to inform them of the fact. There are at least two main lines and a great many branch lines of railway running through the country. I would like to see a great many more; and when I first saw the proposition of the Grand

Trunk Pacific to build a line from North Bay westward, I was very glad to see it, and to give it my support in the Railway Committee; because I believe that in a country as well fitted for settlement as the Northwest, into which so many thousands of people are thronging, it is all the better to havie a fair number of railways so long as they do not interfere with each other, and so long as they are spread over the territories, to help to develop them properly. The grain is carried by these roads, and what becomes of it ? It has been repeated often enough here : we know that the vast bulk of it is sent to the ports of Lake Superior, and we know that it will continue to go there, no matter what railways are built across the country.
It has been so clearly demonstrated that carriage by water is cheaper than carriage by land. No amount of figures could get over the fact that even railways which extend from the furthest west to the furthest east, find it to their advantage, when they come in contact with our great central water-ways, to tranship to those waterways. Not only the Canadian Pacific Railway, but practically all the American roads which have ports on Lakes Michigan and Superior and the other great lakes, transship their grain at these ports, and in many cases millions of bushels of grain are transshipped by railways having eastern connections. That grain is carried by water three times the distance that it is by rail, and transhipped again at Buffalo, simply because the water route is the cheaper. That fact speaks volumes more forcibly than all the fantastic theories hon. gentlemen can invent to justify the building of a railway over that wonderful prairie section between Winnipeg and Quebec, and a railway, as the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) described it, with no greater curves and grades than the lines from Detroit to Buffalo. Such a conception is not one which adds to the reputation of the hon. member for North Norfolk, as a gentleman who pays any attention to the fact, and it was not entertained by the hon. .Minister of Finance, who referred to it in such a manner that showed he was afraid the hon. member for North Norfolk might insist on the government building a road which would cost pretty nearly as much per mile as the Finance Minister estimated for the whole distance. Beyond question there exists now two roads leading to Lake Superior and a water route from Lake Superior, over which may he carried all the grain that can reach the ports of transshipment on that lake. That being the case, I can understand the proposition of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. It is willing simply to connect with its own system in the older provinces, not for the purpose of carrying the grain, which would undoubtedly be carried by it, simply to Lake Superior, but for the purpose of having con-

nections by its own lines between the older provinces and the western provinces.
The second reason given in support of this proposition is that it will help the workers of the older provinces to supply the markets of the North-west, that it will afford an outlet for the manufacturers of Ontario and Quebec who desire to get their goods into the territories. I would like to ask those who advocate the construction of this road from Fort Simpson on the Pacific coast to Winnipeg, then north to Lake Nepi-gon close to the waters of Lake Abitibi, then on to Quebec and Moncton, how that line is going to benefit the toilers of the east. Are these toilers located in the vicinity of Lake Abitibi ? Are the manufacturers situated very largely in the region north of Lake Nepigon ? In the name of common sense, how are the manufacturers of Ontario and Quebec, save those who are located at Quebec city, to reach this road, or to have their goods carried over it to these hundreds of thousands of consumers who are going to the territories ? It will be simply an impossibility unless very expensive cross lines are built.
I believe that in discussing a matter of this kind we should consider the general advantage of Canada, not technically, as in the case of a private Bill, in which this declaration is merely formally made to bring it under the jurisdiction of this parliament, but in the broadest sense of the word. The farmers of Ontario and Quebec have consented to the aid and the assistance of the government being given to the opening up of the North-west, although such a policy operated in a sense to their direct loss. They willingly contributed to this aid and helped on the movement, but they had good and strong reasons for supporting such a policy. They were willing to suffer some financial loss in the first place because it was to the general advantage of the country that the territories should be opened up and our various provinces brought into touch with each other. It was the essence of confederation that that should be done, and those who desired confederation, desired above all things to see it carried out properly. The feeling therefore was almost unanimous on the part of older Canada in supporting a policy of opening up our Northwest. There was another reason which influenced our people. By opening up Manitoba and the territories, they were creating homes for their sons and relatives, and at the same time providing direct communication with them. Further, that was being done by a government which constantly kept the general interests of Canada in view, so that while in the opening up of the North-west there was brought about indirectly a depreciation in the farm values of the east, still the government were at the same time carrying out a policy which helped to develop the east by enlarging the opportunities of the farmers and by lay-

ing the foundation of a broad and strong industrial movement. The policy of opening up our North-west and the policy of encouraging our manufacturing industries went together and constituted that national policy, which our hon. friends opposite have so frequently taken occasion to decry, and have found so much reason to copy. It was that policy which induced the farmers of Ontario and Quebec to contribute so largely out of their substance to the development of our western territories. They knew that the country as a whole would benefit, even though they should have to suffer some loss. But admitting that this proposition may help to develop a remote part of the west, in what way can those gentlemen, who have in such florid language said it would be such a wonderful help to Ontario and Quebec, justify their statement that it is going to develop those parts of Ontario and Quebec, which are now business centres and in which is to be found the great bulk of our population. I submit that when a proposition is made involving so heavy an expenditure, involving such a pledge of the credit of the whole country, it should be one that will assist the country as a whole. When the right hon. the First Minister said that this road would enable the manufacturers in the east to get their products into the west and bring the toilers of the east in touch with consumers of the west, he was stating a proposition which certainly is not justified by the measure he has submitted for our approval. I do not think that we can, in any sense of the word, be called sectional or selfish, if we insist that in any undertaking involving so heavy an expenditure on the whole country, both the east and the west should be considered. But the right hon. gentleman reminds me of a woman who spends most of her time attending missionary meetings and neglects her own home. When somebody asked some ragged children if they knew her, they said, yes she is our mother. And when asked where she was, they replied : she is off attending to the children of the heathen and leaving us children to go to the devil.
I have referred to the expenditure involved. I wish that it were possible to build a road such as the one proposed for the figures given by the First Minister and the Minister of Finance. I wish it were possible for me to persuade myself that this was one of those cases to which the statement of the old Scotchman did not apply, when he said that there were three kinds of lies : white lies, black lies, and the worst lies of all, statistics. The road will not be built for nothing; good money must be paid for it. In fact the Prime Minister not only showed this in his speech introducing the Bill, but I think he laid the foundation for most of the errors that have been made by his followers in discussing it since. He said that we should not only have to advance the 296
money, but we should have to pay interest upon it. And what do we receive in return V We receive interest at the same rate. We pay interest and we receive interest. But we pay out the principal, and how about that ? It is quite clear that the return of the money is not provided for in anything that the right hon. gentleman says. So, when this financial burden is discussed simply from the standpoint of the payment of interest, then the argument rests upon a purely fictitious basis. It seems to me it is not worthy of the position which the Minister of Finance occupies to so utterly ignore the expenditure of principal or to attempt to get round it by his peculiar actuarial method.
I have wondered sometimes as this discussion has gone on, and as the legislation has proceeded in the committee, where on earth this contract came from. Nobody seems willing to father it. We know that the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) did impute the fatherhood of it to one person, Senator Cox. Apparently, there is no justification for placing it on any one else. Personally, I have no knowledge of the matter. But this much I do know-that when the first application came up in the Railway Committee such a contract as this was not suggested, and I believe it was not even thought of. It may have been dreamed of by some, but undoubtedly nothing was said to convey any suggestion of it. We found the first application of the Grand Trunk opposed and opposed particularly by a set of men who had their minds fixed on the project of a railway straight across the country from Quebec. I think I state what is well within the knowledge of members of the committee when I say that the bitterest opponents of the Grand Trunk project were members of this House who advocated the project of a railway westward from Quebec. I am not quarrelling with their right to advocate such a railway; I am simply dealing with the fact. But in some mysterious way the scene was changed. The original proposition was practically withdrawn and a proposition made that was totally opposed to the ideas of the original promoters of the Grand Trunk Pacific as set forth in their circular. According to that circular it is clear that they did not want a line running eastward from Winnipeg. They spoke of a stretch of a thousand miles of that territory being unproductive and of it being a country through which a line should not be run. I admit they are not building it. I do not know how this change of which I speak came about. President Castro of Venezuela tells of a case that arose in his own country. A certain man died leaving a will dividing 'his property among two distant relatives. But two friends who were near him in life, and who had expected bequests in their favour, were much disappointed. They made up a scheme to fix the bequests to their liking before the heirs



came. They succeeded to getting a notary in with them. The three went into the room where the dead man lay, tied a string to his head and gave the end of the string into the hands of one of the would-be heirs. The notary took his pen and asked, do you give so and so to such and such a person V A pull of the string and the head nodded, so tlie notary recorded the bequest. And so the property was distributed until every one had been remembered but tbe notary. The question was then asked, do you give so and so to the notary ? But the man who held the string did not pull. The notary laid down his pen and said, ' this string pulls for everybody, or there is no will.' 1 do not know whether this story illustrates what went on with regard to this contract, but I do know that, in some mysterious way, by some evolution, the working of which is unknown so far as this House is concerned, this contract has been prepared as we have it before the House. It is presented by the Prime Minister backed by reasons that have been almost completely dropped by those on his own side who have spoken. The right lion, gentleman failed to show that there was any emergency or any crisis justifying such a tremendous expenditure, such an extensive mortgaging on the credit of the country on information as meagre and as vague as that in possession of the government, in fact, it would not be too much to say that there is practically no information in their possession. And still, the measure is being pressed before the House. I would join my voice with the voices of those who have pressed upon the government the necessity of referring such an important proposal to the people of the country before finally disposing of it. Six months ago, as I have said, this project had never been thought of. In fact, we might say that no longer than three months ago it had never been thought of. In the general election of 1900 nobody even dreamed of such an undertaking. Yet, surely, the needs of the country were as pressing then as they are now. And, for the government now to lay such a proposal before the House, and force It through on a principle laid down by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) that because the captain says, ' shoot,' he must shoot, I submit, is carrying party government and the discipline of party to an extent that must be, if carried out, be injurious to the country. If there ever was a time when a proposition should be submitted to the electors or when the government that formu lated that proposition should ask for the confidence of the people, it is a time when such a proposition as this is proposed. And it would not delay the work involved in this project to delay the legislation now before us. The government could easily obtain the consent of this House to an appropriation of money to make the necessary surveys and obtain all information to be laid before the House. That must be done before
the work can go on in any case. Even the contract says that delay is to take place. In fact the contract would show that as to the eastern section, which is the one part most open to objection, that the Grand Trunk care little about it. Otherwise, they would not allow the government to stop the work whenever they wanted to. They could if they chose, before attempting that work, go to the country in the meantime under that very clause, and then act according to the mandate of the people, provided they did it in such a way as not to make the country liable for a heavy bill of damages.
There is one other thing that I have not touched upon that has been discussed in recent speeches by hon. gentlemen opposite, and that is the argument that this is a colonization road. What in the name of common sense do we want with a colonization road at the present time, when, according to the statement of the right hon. the Premier, we have more than we can do to supply the wants of the territories that are already opened up to colonization V This road is primarily suggested to meet the wants of the North-west, to meet the wants of the people that are already settled there. No other suggestion was made by the right hon. gentleman. It is for the prairie section, for the mountain section, for the mining section, for the people that are already in the North-west, that this road is primarily to be built; no suggestion of colonization. I do not believe for a single moment that the Prime Minister would have thought it consonant with the gravity of the situation to suggest that we should spend $120,000,000 for a colonization road in northern Ontario and Quebec. Roads of that kind should be undertaken by the provinces, and I am glad to know that the province of Ontario is building its own colonization roads, and it can well do so for a number of years. For our part, we can wait until more is known about that country, and I trust that as more is known, the people will be still more encouraged to build colonization roads, roads that will start from the centres of the older population. How on earth can this road help on the colonization of the central parts of the country ? What centres of population will it touch ? It touches the two terminals, Winnipeg and Quebec only, and everything that is carried into that country or carried out of it would have to go either to Quebec or to Winnipeg, until a few costly cross roads have been built, and these cross roads will form the best colonization roads. I hope sincerely that some day they will be undertaken, that some day we will see this road now proposed going from Winnipeg to Quebec on the shortest possible line. When that day comes, I think it will be built by a private corporation, using its own money, or better still, be built by the government, owning and operating its own road, instead of being built by the government and hand-

ed over to a private corporation who does not Want it, who does not expect to make any money out of it, and who gives no valid undertaking that they will operate it. While the North-west is filling up, we will have ample opportunity to explore the routes for these colonization roads, and there will be ample time for some future parliament to discuss the question of a road from the east to the west across that northern section.
It is not because we have no faith in the country that we oppose the proposition embodied in this Bill; it is not because we have no desire to see the country settled ; it is not at all because we have no desire to see trade developed, rather the reverse. The whole proposition as It stands before us is one that will give us the least benefit at the greatest possible outlay. We cannot undertake any such expenditure as this without imperilling our ability to engage in any other public work for many years to come.
Notwithstanding some of the criticisms that have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite of the scheme propounded by the leader of the opposition, I submit that it is one that will appeal to every business man, and every citizen, and every person looking to the interest of the country as a whole, and desiring to see a more economical use made of our money. It is not to the expenditure of the money that we are opposed, as our leader has said, but it is to the way the money is to be expended, and the little benefit that the country will reap from it. In view of the fact that our water routes will for years to come, possibly for all time, be the regulators of railways from the North-west to the east, in view of the fact that they will be the means, probably for all time to come, so far as we can now see, of carrying the surplus products of the west to the east for consumption and exportation, in view of the fact that we have in the past undertaken the development of our water-ways and to improve the navigation of the lakes in order to secure cheaper transportation of goods, in view of the fact that only recently the government, wisely in my opinion, in order to make transportation still cheaper from the west, took away the canal tolls and made those canals to a greater extent than before a benefit to the country as a whole, and principally to the North-west-in view of all these facts, I say the immediate necessity of this proposed new railway has not been made out. Surely no person will say that we have brought these water-ways entirely up-to-date, that we have made them as efficient as possible for all the purposes for which they are required. We must remember that in years to come, if we do our duty by the people of this country, we will have to expend large sums of money in improving these water-ways in different directions. 1 submit that a proposition that involves the 2964
building of our own roads, to be owned and operated by the government, is one that will not only have the best results at present, but will in future lead to Infinitely better results. It may be that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee), though at present perhaps it is somewhat academic, can in the near future be beneficially applied. That Is a principle which, sooner or later, we will have to face, and it is well perhaps that we are face to face with the general principle even now. It is with very great pleasure indeed that I heard the leader of the party to which I have the honour to belong, make the proposition that practically meant government control of freights east and west, over a government line owned and operated by the country. If there is any way by which we can get the produce of the west to our own seaports, it will be by means of the control of their transport from the time those products are put on the train. If there is any way by which we can most effectually control rates, it is by having a government road which will establish the rates for all other lines running in the same direction.
The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) said that this was a red letter day for Canada. , So it is, Sir. We are now in the full midsummer of our prosperity, a prosperity that was established by the wise and fruitful work of the statesmen who preceded the hon. gentlemen now sitting on the government benches. You cannot have a harvest without a sowing, and if the sowing is not wisely done, the harvest will amount to but little. It says but little for the knowledge of national development possessed by hon. gentlemen opposite when they call attention to the spectacular results of this midsummer, and forget the work by which the prosperity of this midsummer has been brought about. It is this very fact, I believe, which makes it so difficult for hon. gentlemen opposite now to rise to a sense of their duties and responsibilities. It is one thing to enjoy a harvest from the work of the men of the past, and it is another thing to use that harvest wisely. It is to be hoped that the party now in power will use its opportunity in such a way as to help on the general prosperity we now enjoy, instead of giving it a setback. It will not use unwisely or extravagantly the revenues that come in, it will not use unwisely the opportunities that it now has on account of the great credit the country enjoys, but It will use them in such a way that development will go on upon the old lines, that the old will not be neglected for the new, that one part of the country will not be set against another, but that the development, the growth and the prosperity of the whole country will move harmoniously together. For this reason it is a matter of duty that causes one to oppose such a proposition as that which has been made by the right hon. leader of

the government in this Bill, and to support the alternative policy proposed by the hon. leader of the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, coming a little late in this debate I wish to say at the outset that the character of the debate has appeared to me to be higher than any I have yet listened to in this House since I became a member of it, and that I scarcely wonder at it when I consider the measure which has been Introduced by the government and which is the subject of debate at this particular time. A subject that involves the expenditure of such a large sum of money and the giving of such a large guarantee, a subject that involves the building of a transcontinental line over which the freight of Canada is to go in Canadian channels and to Canadian seaports and which will not only develop new parts of Canada, but which will be a benefit to Canada as a whole, is certainly one that should invite the best possible debating talent in this House and I certainly congratulate those who have preceded me on the magnificent character of the speeches which have already been made. I desire, however, to differ from much that several hon. members on the other side of the House have said in reference to this measure. It would appear from what they have said that the people scarcely expected such a measure to be introduced by this government, but, on the contrary it seems to me that the record of the government has already shown it to be of a character that would be very apt to introduce such a scheme as this for the general advantage of Canada. When we look over the record of a few short years of this government we see how the anticipations of the people have been answered by the introduction of this scheme. It is said that every progressive government is constantly undertaking new duties or performing old ones more thoroughly and efficiently and when we look at the record of the past few years of the government which is in power in almost every direction, in almost every department we see how apt that statement is as applied to them. They introduced a tariff for revenue in 1897, and we see how that tariff has stimulated trade in this country until in this year we have the enormous surplus of $14,000,000 and we have on record the fact additional that many millions of dollars of our debt are to be paid off as a result. When they introduced the preferential tariff they introduced, I believe, a patriotic measure, when they introduced postal reduction they introduced another patriotic measure and when they perfected a successful immigration policy which is bringing people by thousands into this country they again showed their ability to grasp the situation as it in this country. So that in one direction and another, this government have shown themselves to be a successful government and I have little or Mr. LAVEL.L.
n'o doubt that when the people learned that the government were about to introduce a measure looking to the construction of a transcontinental railway, that as the government had taken up one measure after another that had operated to the prosperity of this country, that as they had been successful in every measure they had taken up, as has been shown in the increase of trade, in the increase of prosperity and in the increase of the population, they expected that the measure which they were taking up at this time would be a measure which would redound to the present and future advantage and prosperity of this great country of ours.
Now, in the first place, I desire to correct a statement which was made last evening by the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier), in regard to the question of the exemption from customs duties on supplies coming into this country for the construction of this railway. The answer to his statement last evening is set out so fully, so cogently and so definitely in the speech of the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) at page 8582 of ' Hansard ' that I will not attempt in my own words to discuss the matter, but, I wiil give the House his statement of the matter. The hon. Minister of Finance said:
But, Sir. as this road is to he built by contractors, and the contractors will have to tender for the work, they will receive no exemption whatever. Therefore any man who has anything to do with the construction of that road, if he imports materials, he will have to pay the duty, and if he buys the goods in Canada the Canadian manufacturer will have the benefit of the duty in so far as that is of any advantage to him. The Minister of Customs calls my attention to the fact that the government will let the construction of this road by contract and that the contractors will have to pay customs duties on the materials they import. I think I stated that. Of course, if you could imagine such a thing as the government building this road themselves, and if the government were importing materials, they would, as in the case of the Intercolonial Railway, not enter these goods at the customs house. They would be for the government service. But I say that even there we do not as respects the eastern division, take any advantage of that, because we provide that it shall be built by tender and contract, and the contractors will not have any exemption, but will have to buy the goods in Canada or else pay the duties if they see fit to import them. When we come to the western division, we deal with the company. They will build the road, and will not have any exemption in any shape or form. They will not be at liberty to import a penny's worth of goods without paying the same duty that is paid by any private individual. The grant in the way of exemption from customs duties in the contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was a vast privilege. I do not attempt to compute it in money, but I am sure that it would run into a vast sum. We do not give any exemptions of any sort.
There is n complete and definite answer to the statement made by the hon. membei-for Toronto last evening.

Would the hou. gentleman give us the section under which he arrives
at that conclusion ?

Section No. 17 :
No addition shall be made to the cost of construction or to the capital of construction account in respect of customs duties in cases where there is direct importation of material or supplies by the government.
Now, Sir, we have been hearing during tiiis discussion a good deal from hon. members on the other side of the House and very much to my surprise from hon. members from the province of Ontario about the condition of New Ontario. It has been sought to belittle the reports that the Ontario government had from time to time put out and the reports which are based upon the surveys of the surveyors they sent out several years ago. I have been very much surprised to see hon. members from the province of Ontario seeking to belittle New Ontario and to belittle these reports, because, if they recollect that when the provincial contest was on a little over a year ago and when Mr. Whitney was in New Ontario making his speeches, this whole question was a matter of considerable controversy in that province. I think it is well known to the members of this House that for many years past the policy of the Liberal party under the present premier particularly, 1ms been for the development and colonization of New Ontario. Now I may say that has been the policy of both parties in Ontario, and I find what ought to be an unanswerable argument to those hon. members on the other side of the House who seek to belittle New Ontario and who seek to belittle the reports which the Ontario government has put out because these reports are not signed and because they give simply the substance of what the surveyors reported, and who on this account seek to make out that these reports are not authentic. That was not the position taken by the Conservative party a year and a quarter ago during the provincial contest. I propose to read some extracts from the ' Mail and Empire ' editorials of that time to show that not merely was it not disputed that New Ontario was wonderfully rich in agricultural resources aud was wonderfully rich in mineral and timber resources, hut that the charge then was that Mr. Ross and the Liberal party were not realizing the extent of the riches of that country, and that they were not alive to the opportunities that were presented to them of developing and colonizing it. but that they were derelict in their duty in that respect. Here are some extracts from the Toronto ' Mail ' which go to show the position of the Conservative party in Ontario at that time. In the * Mail ' of May 8. 1902, we find the following in an editorial under the caption, 'Ontario's forward movement':
In the great clay belt, stretching from Quebec to the Thunder Bay district, are 24,500 miles of unbroken farming land, where settlers would build up a new province.
Again, in the issue of May 9, we read this:
We have much to gain in business by the development of the newer parts of Ontario.
Again, under date of May 15, it says :
Nature has decreed that the expansion of Ontario must be northward, but a narrow and incompetent administration has hitherto maintained barriers against the onward march of settlement. The mistake of the government has been that it accepted the dictum of Mr. Ross that the soil of the north was barren and the climate unfavourable, and made no effort to open up the country, while at the same time it shut the settlers out of vast stretches that it handed over to the corporations. As a matter of fact New Ontario is south of a large portion of Dakota, and is more fit for agriculture and stock grazing than prairie lands of the west.
But in the issue of May 17, perhaps the most comprehensive statement appears :
The government refused to make a move until 1900, when several exploring parties were sent out.
These are the exploring parties, upon whose statement the report which was laughed at by hon. gentlemen opposite during this debate, was founded. The ' Mail ' goes on :
They have reported that there is an almost unbroken stretch of good farming land, a great clay belt stretching from the Quebec boundary to the Thunder bay district, comprising an area of 24,509 miles. Until i.his proof was forced upon him Mr. G. W. Ross maintained that the soil of New Ontario was barren and the climate unfavourable. Yet nearly as large a province, fit in every sense for profitable development. lies in our vacant north land as we have in old Ontario. This territory is in part south of Dakota, and its climate is less severe than that of the Canadian west. The whole country, we are assured, is a network of lakes, rivers and streams, well-wooded, teeming with game, and specially adapted to agriculture and stock raising. It is, moreover, well stocked with minerals, and has abundance of waterpower for industrial purposes. ... It will be a big thing for southern Ontario to have a New Ontario in the north, growing up to contain perhaps millions in the near future. It will give a stimulus to our cities and our industries. and will afford splendid openings for our young men. We are of course glad to witness the progress of the west, but we shall be happier and better off besides when Mr. Whitney inaugurates and carries to a successful issue the policy that will populate Ontario.
These are the statements of the ' Mail ' newspaper in reference to the very reports issued by the Ontario government which are sneered at by the members of the opposition as furnishing no proof of the wonderful fertility and resources of that great New Ontario which this transcontinental scheme will do so much to develop.
Since 1 came into this House I have heard a great deal about the development of the west, and no one desires more than I do

that the west should be developed. I am perfectly well aware that for many years past the development of the west has been perhaps more attributable to the influx into that country of people from Ontario than to almost any other cause. The province of Ontario has given many thousands of her people to the development of the west, and we are glad of it. We want to see Oauada as a whole developed. But now that the North-west Territories are getting a splendid start, now that not only people from Ontario, but from the old land and the United States, are going into the North-west in large numbers, we in Ontario are beginning to think that it is time that we should look a little to the development of the newer portions of our own province.
Prior to the local elections of last year, Mr. Ross laid down his policy in a number of paragraphs, among which this was stated as a prominent feature:
The early settlement of the unoccupied lands of the province by colonization and by the projection of railways into New Ontario.
When the legislature met he crystallized that paragraph iuto an Act, and under that Act the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway is now being constructed. And it seems to me that it was most opportune that that railway should have been commenced this year. When the proposed transcontinental railway shall be completed across the country, this provincial railway, now being constructed by the government of Ontario, will tap that railway, and so not only bring the whole of New Ontario into connection with the older parts of the province, but place Ontario in probably a better position than any other province of the Dominion to send supplies of all kinds to Manitoba and the North-west, and in that way serve the interests of the people of Ontario at large. Let us look at the preamble of the Act of the Ontario legislature for the construction of the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario Railway, and see how it accords with the preamble of the Act for the construction of the national transcontinental railway. The preamble of the Ontario Act reads as follows :
Whereas exploration of the province has shown that in that district of Ontario which lies between Lake Nipissing and Lakje Abitibi and north-westerly from Lake Temiskaming there are large areas of arable land well Stted for settlement and extensive tracts of merchantable pine and other valuable timber, and deposits of ores and minerals which are expected, upon development, to add greatly to the wealth of the province ; and whereas the said district is now difficult of acess from the lack of railway communication ; and whereas an increasing' number of settlers are taking up lands in portions of the said district ; and whereas it is in the public interest that the said district should be, at as early a date as possible, brought into communication with the existing lines of railway.
I desire here to express my appreciation of this Bill. The province of Ontario has, we Mr. SUTHERLAND (Essex).
believe, for many years past been a pioneer in legislation in almost every direction. If time permitted, I could show how measure after measure which has been passed by the Ontario legislature has later on been imitated, not only by the various provinces of the Dominion, but by some of the states to the south of us. This Ontario Bill provides that the railway shall be constructed by a commission. That and other provisions in the Bill have perhaps suggested one or two of the clauses which appear in the measure now before this House. I have read the preamble of that Bill just to show, by way of comparison, how far it resembles the preamble of the Bill before this House, which reads as follows :
Whereas, by reason of the growth in population and the rapid development in the productiveness and trade of Canada, and especially of the western part thereof, and with a view to the opening up of new territory available for settlement, both in the eastern provinces and in the west, and the affording of transportation facilities for such territory, and for other reasons, the necessity has arisen for the construction of a national transcontinental railway.
It seems to me that these two measures are supplementary of each other, so far as the province of Ontario is concerned ; that just as Ontario projected its railway for the purpose of developing the magnificent heritage which we have in the north, and which is awaiting colonization and population, so the project now before this House is brought forward just at a time to enable the Ontario railway to connect with it near the height of land, and so to enable the province to populate and colonize that splendid clay belt very much faster than she could otherwise have done. The scheme, it seems to me, so far as Ontario is concerned, amounts to this. One of these days, in the not very distant future, the province of Ontario would have had to build on its own account, and along this very direction, a railway of a colonization character. But by "this scheme, many years earlier perhaps than we would have built it, and without its costing one dollar more, perhaps not nearly so much as it would have cost if constructed by the province alone, we will have this road which otherwise we would have had to build ourselves, built by the Dominion, and in that way will reap an immense advantage.
Another feature which commends it to me is this. The various provinces, except perhaps the province of Ontario, have very considerable debts to meet. The debts of some of these provinces are very large, and the provinces are beginning to look out in various directions for the means to meet them. There are methods being adopted in Ontario to-day which were not followed some years ago. One of the merits of this scheme is this, that instead of the various provinces having to build railways of this kind themselves, and in that way pledge

their credit and assume a responsibility which many of them cannot very well afford, the Dominion will finance largely the matter, so that instead of each province having to pay directly, as it would have to do, if it financed the matter itself, it will only pay indirectly its contribution to the cost by means of customs duties and the like. That will be an advantage to every province of the confederation.
I did not intend, Mr. Speaker, to speak at length in this discussion at all; but coming from Ontario I considered it advisable that I should point out some of the advantages which will accrue to that province from this scheme. I recognize, as every speaker on this side has done, that' this is a great scheme for the advantage of the Dominion as a whole. Much has been done in the past few years to attract attention to the Dominion. Various things have caused us to be advertised and become known. Population and capital, these two things which this young country has so long needed, are beginning to flow in more than at any period within our history, and I believe that when this scheme becomes understood, this movement will receive still greater impetus. The outside world will realize that we are alive to our responsibilities and following the example set by other nations. We find Great Britain talking about spending $15,000,000 to connect Glasgow and Edinburgh for trade and imperial purposes. In the very heart of Egypt, she is spending $20,000,000 on the construction of a great dam for the purpose of irrigation, which, it is estimated, will add $25,000,000 to the value of lands in that country. In Australia, we find that the government of that colony has commenced the construction of a transcontinental line across the whole island. In India, the British government is spending millions of dollars on canals, and in the neighbouring republic the great Panama canal scheme is being actively promoted. In almost every country we find the people realizing their responsibilities and investing large sums in gigantic enterprises, in order to attract trade and population. Canada must not lag behind. We have immense resources awaiting development. All we need is population and capital, and this scheme, coupled with the other undertakings which the government have accomplished, will attract still more capital and population to our shores, and this young country will become, what we all hope to see it at an early day, one of the strongest, most prosperous, enterprising and powerful nations in the world.
I could hardly sit down without saying a word about the railway company which is associated with this scheme. The old Grand Trunk Railway has done much for many parts of Canada, particularly the western part of Ontario. It went into that section practically as a colonization railway. It is to the Grand Trunk Railway that is due the first settlement of western Ontario,
and when it is known that that section of country has become one of the most fertile, best settled and most progressive of the whole Dominion, one can realize what will result from the activity and enterprise of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in New Ontario, New Quebec, New British Columbia, and New New Brunswick. One can realize what will result when this great, strong, enterprising concern, assisted by this government, will open up these new portions of Canada. Just as it has made western Ontario prosperous and successful, so it will develop these new sections, and in this way be a great boom to the people of Canada.
We are just now having a great meeting in Montreal of leading men from all parts of the empire, assembled there to discuss imperial matters. From Montreal they will go out through the length and breadth of Canada to see this young country, and the more they learn about it, the more they realize that we have arisen to the measure of our responsibility and are seeking to construct a great Canadian transcontinental railway, which will redound to the credit of the empire as a whole, the more they will have confidence in our future and be prepared to invest their money and capital in the development of Canada.
The more I have studied this contract and listened to this debate, the more I am convinced of the merits of this scheme. In his opening speech, my right hon. friend the , First Minister showed how this scheme was intended to serve broad, imperial interests. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) and the Minister of the Interior dilated upon the practical necessity for this railway and its utility in the interests of the country. The Minister of Finance showed, in the most practical, clear manner, that every financial arrangement was provided for in this contract; and when the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Russell) spoke, he proved abundantly, from the weight of authority and experience, that the most efficient system of government owned railways was when the railway owned by the government was operated by some practical business concern, such as the Grand Trunk Railway. And when I heard the Minister of Justice going through the clauses of that contract-and I appreciated perhaps as a lawyer his statement of the case more than that of any of the other ministers-when 1 heard him go through these clauses and saw how the interests of the country, in clear, concise, plain phraseology, were safeguarded in every way,. I came to the absolute conclusion that no scheme ever put forward by any government had the interest of the people at large so well protected.

As this is Friday evening, Mr. Speaker, and it is now half past ten, I think we ought to adjourn the debate; and with the consent of the hon. gentleman who is leading the House, I would move the adjournment of the debate.
I think we might go one hour longer.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman who Is a military man is perhaps inclined to he rather strict and has more endurance than I have. After being here all day and up to this hour at night, I do not feel in a condition to do justice to the subject, and I would ask the hon. gentleman to allow us to adjourn. For a man of my years, it would be rather an arduous task to address the House at this hour.
Since the hon. gentleman makes an appeal of that kind, and as he is a very old personal friend of mine, I think we must give way and consent to the adjournment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and 'debate adjourned.
On motion of the Minister of Militia and Defence, House adjourned at 10.30 p.m.
Monday, August 24, 1903.
